Right Hon, L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister): Mr. Speaker, I should like to move, seconded by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), the resolution of which notice appears at page 11 of the order paper, as follows:
That on and after Wednesday, December 12, 1951, until the end of the session, the house shall meet at 11 o'clock in the morning of each sitting day and that, in addition to the usual intermission at 6.15 o'clock, p.m., there shall be an intermission everyday from 1 to 2.30 o'clock, p.m., except on Friday, when the intermission shall be from 1 to 2 o'clock, p.m.; and every Wednesday and Friday until the end of the session the house shall meet from 8 to 10 o'clock, p.m.
I feel that it is the hope of many members of parliament that without unduly rushing anything we might complete the business that is to be dealt with perhaps even this week, and if not this week by early in next week so that hon. members, including those who reside at great distances from Ottawa, may have plenty of time to reach their homes before Christmas day. I hope that this motion will meet with unanimous approval of the house.	' . * ' " ,

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS ON AND AFTER WEDNESDAY, DECEMBER 12
speechtext:
I am not prepared to give unanimous approval to a motion of this kind for a particular reason among others. Early in the session there was an indication that after several years of discussion there was going to be a committee on defence expenditures set up at this present session. In spite of the importance of that committee it began to sit only last week and for reasons which I need not discuss but which I do not regard as valid it has held only intermittent meetings.
The committee met again this morning and adjourned until Thursday. I would suggest that if there is any other reason why we should meet in an orderly way and not hasten the proceedings of this house to the point where business cannot be dealt with expeditiously by members who wish to sit on committees as well it is that there should be a report from the committee on defence expenditures before this house rises.
The motion before us is obviously for the purpose of getting work done so that the predictions that have been offered that we might terminate the sittings this week can be fulfilled. I believe that it is immensely important that the time of our sitting remain as it is so that hon. members who attend committees may also have an opportunity to sit in the house. A number of the committees are still sitting and these are all important committees. There is the committee on defence expenditures; there is the committee on radio; there are committees on other matters, and I think hon. members should still attach some importance to public accounts, which committee is still sitting.
There cannot be that attention to the work of these committees and also attention to the business of the house that the nature of the work of the house justifies if this motion is adopted. I urge strongly that it should not be adopted and that we continue to meet at the hours that have been set.
There is another reason. I think members of this house should be given an opportunity to digest the reports in order to be able to present their views thereon. It is perfectly clear at the moment that they will not have the slightest chance to examine these reports and express their opinion if this course is followed. Therefore I oppose the motion and I hope that it will not pass.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
subtopic: DISCONTINUANCE OF IRO
speechtext: I did not hear the radio comment, Mr. Speaker, but I suppose it was a version of the story which appeared in the newspapers. speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, December 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. Robert Cauchon for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Argue, as amended.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this house we have been engaged for some time in debating a motion that a humble address be presented to His Excellency the Governor General, Field Marshal the Right Hon. the Viscount Alexander of Tunis. It so happens, sir, that today is the birthday of His Excellency the Governor General. I know I am speaking on behalf of all hon. members of this house when I extend to him birthday felicitations, greetings and good wishes. A man great in war and in peace, the manner in which he has discharged his responsibilities as Governor General has made him justly popular everywhere in this Dominion of Canada.
There have been amendments and subamendments, the latest of which was moved on Wednesday last. For the first time in more than a generation, in order to water down an amendment that would constitute a motion of non-confidence in His Excellency's advisers, a member supporting the government has moved a subamendment which was, to say the least, constitutionally unusual. I believe the result of that subamendment, regular in its form as it was and in order as declared by Your Honour, has been to place the government of this country in a quagmire of difficulty. I intend, if I may, to refer to the only examples that exist of an amendment or a subamendment along the lines of the one in question. When I do so, I want to give my thanks to the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) for his collaboration and study in connection with this matter.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: North Centre.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It is usually North Centre who deals with the rules, but this time I refer to South Centre, a new member who has come into the house but recently, and who adds
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker that strength and ability to the house which able and qualified men bring to our deliberations.
I believe it is worth bringing to the attention of the government that an examination of the Journals of this house indicates that from 1867 until 1902 the practice was followed of moving a resolution to the effect that a humble address be presented to the Governor General. The formal address was followed by a series of paragraphs repeating almost word for word the corresponding statements which appeared in the speech from the throne. From 1888 until 1896 the practice was to put the question for each paragraph of the resolu* tion, and it was discontinued.
The custom up to 1895 was to refer to a special committee of the house the drafting of an address to His Excellency or to His Majesty the King. In 1903 a short form of address was adopted which is the one in effect now. It is interesting to note that. Between 1867 and 1902 only two amendments to the resolution were ever considered. The first of these was in 1893 and was an amendment by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, then in opposition, and the amendment was defeated. The seoond amendment occurred in 1899, and that is one similar in nature to that moved by the hon. member for The Battle-fords (Mr. Bater). That amendment proposed adding a tenth paragraph to the resolution and suggested the appointment of a judicial commission to investigate alleged malpractices in the administration of the Yukon. A subamendment was moved by the government supporters expressing confidence in the commissioner of the Yukon. The subamendment carried and was added as paragraph ten of the resolution.
Someone will immediately say that what the hon. member for The Battlefords has done, even though it is as far back as 1899, indicated that we have the right to do it now. At the time that subamendment was moved general procedure was different from what it is now. As I pointed out a moment ago, in 1903 the humble address that we now send to His Excellency was then adopted. From 1903 to the present day the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne has occupied more time of the house than it had previous to the adoption of the short form of address. In the period between 1903 and June 1951, 35 amendments and 30 subamendments, a total of 65, that have been found in order or have not been challenged, have been proposed to the address in reply to the speech from the throne. In all those 65 amendments never has there been a case, since the alteration in the procedure connected

The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker with the address from the throne, in which a government member has moved a subamendment. We therefore have to turn to Britain and examine its constitutional practice and history.
The practice in the British House of Commons appears to have been the same as that which is now followed in Canada. The short form in reply to the speech from the throne was adopted in Britain in 1891, and amendments thereto have always been considered as motions of want of confidence. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) gave his imprimatur to that viewpoint when, on October 15 last, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) moved an amendment and asked that there be a free vote in the House of Commons, and said that there was no intention to have the amendment to the motion considered as a vote of non-confidence. As reported at page 33 of Hansard the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said:
If It is not a motion of no confidence it probably is not in order . . .
He had said earlier that it was a matter for the Speaker to decide. In the fifteenth edition of Erskine May's Parliamentary Practice, 1950, there are only two references to amendments to the address being passed in Britain. One of those occurred in 1924 and resulted in the immediate resignation of the government I repeat, Mr. Speaker, what I said a while ago, that this government is in a procedural quagmire. I think they are in the position that the psalmist referred to when he said: "In the net which they hid is their own foot taken". Apparently they devised this form of adulteration which removes from the opposition the right to place before parliament and have parliament vote on amendments that are non-confidence amendments. We have gone far enough along the way of the one-party state. We in this opposition and all future oppositions should not be denied the right to introduce specific motions of non-confidence and have them voted upon in the house irrespective of the difficulties or the mental exercise that may be caused to some of the members for having to vote on an amendment which they would like to support but which their political persuasion does not permit them to do.
I believe that before we are through with this matter, if we are to restore some degree of constitutional regularity to what has happened, I think the government will have to do something similar to that which was done in 1894. Then a Liberal government was in power and Lord Roseberry was Prime Minister. Sir William Harcourt was leader of the house. An amendment was put forward 
by a private member on the opposition side dealing with the subject of restricting the power of the House of Lords. Some of the government members then had a higher degree of independence than has been characteristic of government members at other times and in other places, and they voted for the amendment. The result was that the amendment to the address was supported on a vote of 147 to 145.
If you read Hansard and the London Times of that period you will find that, for two or three days, there was an unusual degree of excitement in the house. The government was embarrassed. Governments sometimes became embarrassed in those days as a result of constitutional difficulties in which they found themselves. There was no precedent. Mr. Balfour of the official opposition, who was always a master of understatement, said that this was "an unexampled position in our parliamentary history". The government did not feel they should resign. But the government found itself in a position where it could not submit the address in its amended form to the king. Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, His Excellency receiving the following address, as it will read if the subamendment passes:
May it please Your Excellency:
We, His Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the House of Commons of Canada, in parliament assembled, beg leave to offer our humble thanks to Your Excellency for the gracious speech which Your Excellency has addressed to both houses of parliament; but this house regrets the serious difficulties encountered by the western farmers in harvesting their crops, and commends Your Excellency's advisers for the continuing attention they have given to the problems caused thereby, and is confident that effective measures will continue to be taken to help the farmers in meeting these problems.
When His Majesty's representative receives that message, it will have one qualification: it will be unique in parliamentary history. In effect it says: This is a motion of confidence and regret but in voting for the motion of non-confidence we want at the same time to say that we have confidence in the government. We are slipping a little but we will not fall in expressing our confidence in the government. My submission is that if the government and the members supporting it vote affirmatively in connection with the amendment of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), as amended by the hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Bater), it will be tantamount to saying that they have no confidence in the government while at the same time saying that they have.

speechtext:
In the British parliament, to extricate themselves from the unusual situation the government had to ask the assistance of the official opposition, with the result that the house voted down the main motion as amended and subsequently moved a new address expressed in terms similar to the original. And thus, though humiliated, a precedent was not established of the government amending its own address.
That, sir, is the position in which, as I see it, the government is placed. After all, the form of address if the amendment of the hon. member for The Battlefords is adopted is bound to be unusual. It will be a departure from a hundred years of parliamentary practice in Great Britain. It will be a departure from over fifty-five years of parliamentary procedure in this country.
The situation that occurred in Great Britain in 1894 occurred, I point out, not with the connivance, assistance or condonation of the government, or with the assistance of a government member. It arose by an amendment moved by an opposition member. I suggest, sir, that the government take immediate action to remove the anomalous situation created by the subamendment, in the interests of sound and constitutional parliamentary procedure and in order to preserve future parliaments from a ruling that, while sound and unchallengeable, will have the effect of removing from the opposition the right that oppositions should have, and that should surely not be denied even though the government has an overwhelming majority-the right to move amendments on specific matters and to have the amendments voted on; otherwise a precedent will be created that future
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker parliaments will always be subject, on amendments expressing non-confidence, to subamendments by government members designed to make them palatable to government members by a substituted form of adulteration such as .will take place if the subamendment is passed. I suggest that this subamendment, in its present form, is an example of a trend indicative of an allpowerful government which would remove from the opposition the last surviving right it has in parliament, that of moving a clear-cut motion of non-confidence.
I pass on now to discuss the excessive load of taxation the Canadian people are carrying today, in consequence of the bad guesses made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and his advisers a few short months ago. Before proceeding further I may say that this amendment could have been moved a considerable time ago, but it was not moved until the Minister of Finance returned to Canada, after having represented this country abroad. One of the pleasant amenities of parliament is that while we all cannot and should not see eye to eye, and parliament could not exist with only one party, nevertheless, regardless of party we do endeavour to maintain those friendly relationships without which parliament would be chaotic and ineffective. I know every member of the opposition joins with me in welcoming the Minister of Finance back to this country. He will have the opportunity today to answer personally for whatever may be said regarding the overtaxation that has taken place here during recent months.
The other day in opening my remarks I said that no Canadian would object to paying a fair share of the taxes necessary to run this country and to build up our defences. I am sure the minister has been back in Canada long enough to find out that everywhere in this country people are aroused, as never before, owing to the fact that in the past several months hundreds of millions of dollars more than required for civil expenditures and for defence have been collected by the government.
It is not as though a warning had not been given in this connection. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), and the financial critic of this party, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), when the new taxation measures were brought in last spring warned as to what would happen, and pointed out that there was no need for this extra taxation. We objected to the increase in sales tax from 8 to 10 per cent. We said that could only have the effect of increasing the high
1722	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker cost of living, applying as it does to household furnishings, clothing, shoes and other needs. Not only would it increase the price index, but it would increase the cost of living; for in my opinion the index number does not represent the degree to which, in an individual case, the cost of living has gone up in this country.
The leader of the opposition and those who followed him in the debate objected to the 15 per cent tax on refrigerators, stoves, washing machines and the like. We objected to the 20 per cent added to income tax, the so-called defence surtax, and joined in support of a motion moved by hon. members to my left stating that that added 20 per cent income tax should not apply to people in the low income tax brackets. On every one of these matters the government and its supporters voted in unity for the additional taxation.
We dealt with the extraordinarily heavy tax imposed upon cigarettes and tobaccos. We endeavoured to show that there was no need for this extra taxation. The answer of the Minister of Finance was that the best estimates that he and his advisers could give would be that the surplus for the fiscal year would not be over $30 million. The government talks about using the surplus for the purpose of discharging debt, but they never said anything about that last spring when they secured the approval of parliament for additional taxation. There was no mandate on the part of parliament to impose upon the Canadian people excessive, overwhelming and unwarranted taxation at a time when the cost of living was as high as it was then, so as to have a surplus for debt retirement.
Yet, because of the government majority, numerous as it is, these taxes were imposed. And now the people of this country find themselves in many cases caught between the squeeze of rising prices and high taxation. I think everywhere in this country the Canadian taxpayer would like to know where members of the House of Commons stand on this question.
I intend to move in amendment the following:
And further regrets that Your Excellency's advisers continue to collect unnecessarily high taxes beyond requirements and have failed at the present session of parliament to relieve the people from unnecessary, burdensome and unjustified taxation.
The latest report of the bureau of statistics indicates that the cost of living is still rising. A major factor in this increasing cost of living is a government policy of taxation far in excess of its requirements.
It has usually been said that high taxation siphons off savings and meets the onrush of prices and inflation. With the government


today collecting hundreds of millions of dollars more than it needs for its purposes, this extra taxation is inflationary in its operation.
I repeat that Canadians are willing, in the interests of national defence, to stand behind the government and parliament, and will pay the taxation needed. But surely there is no justification, without a mandate from parliament, for collecting from every person in this country in a period of seven months $45 more than required for the purposes of governing the country, developing the nation, building up our defences and playing our fair part, and paying our share in the international sphere.
When the Minister of Finance announced his budget on April 10 last he estimated that the total expenditures for the present fiscal year would amount to $3,700 million and it was upon that basis that he was budgeting. The estimate was $1,664 million for defence; $1,923 million for non-defence, and $113 million for supplementary estimates. As it turned out the supplementaries amounted to $195,172,000.
To meet these increased expenditures the Minister of Finance announced taxation changes designed to produce actual additional revenues of about $405 million, which he estimated would result in a surplus of approximately $30 million for the entire year. But with every passing month the surplus gets greater and the government boasts of a month by month increase in the revenue. If revenues are maintained at the present level, and there is every probability that they will foe not only maintained but increased, the gross revenue for this year will exceed $4,000 million.
Do not let the government answer that by saying that the surplus is caused by the fact that they have not been able to get their defence mobilization under way as it was anticipated. Allowing for the expenditure of every dollar provided by parliament for defence purposes this year, and irrespective of the fact that government is behind in its defence expenditures, if they expend every dollar for which the minister budgeted the surplus on the basis of the present monthly increases in revenue over expenditures will amount to at least $230 million at the end of the fiscal year instead of $30 million as estimated.
This situation is serious. If the present rate of surplus continues to pile up month by month at the present rate it will amount to around $900 million at the end of the fiscal year. On the other hand, if the government even at this time were to expand its expenditures for defence to the amount that

was budgeted we would still have at the end of the year a surplus of $200 million beyond that estimated by the minister.
I want to point out that reduced expenditures for defence are not the only contributing factor to that huge surplus now being taken from the Canadian people under what I believe to be exorbitant taxes. The revenues for the entire fiscal year after additional increased taxes were levied were estimated to reach $3,730 million, which would result in a surplus of $30 million. Ordinary revenues for the month of October amounted to $352 million, making a total of ordinary revenues for the first seven months of $2,147,967,000 as compared with just a little under $1,500 million for the same period last year.
What does all this mean? It simply means that either the government guessed wrong or they did not properly place before parliament the facts when the support of parliament was secured for this extra taxation. I should like to read an article by Austin F. Cross, which I am sure every hon. member of the government has read, which appeared in the December issue of New Liberty magazine and in which the matter is set forth clearly, distinctly and factually. He points out that the government may call it taxation that has provided so large a surplus but in reality it is taking from the Canadian people money that parliament never considered was being voted, and that that is unjustifiable having regard to the estimates made for national defence and for civil expenditures last April.
It may be said that we are not overtaxed, but I would refer hon. members to figures which appeared recently in the Financial Post. In the article a comparison is made between United States and Canadian federal taxation and it shows that we in Canada are paying far more in taxes on many of the necessities required by the ordinary person than is paid in the United States. It compares the taxation on cigarettes, and I shall refer to that in a moment. It compares the taxation on automobiles, automobile parts, beverages, blankets, household requirements, and all of those things by the hundred which are used by the ordinary people.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What about income tax?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I shall let my hon. friend put the figures on the record with regard to income tax. In the United States capital gains are taxed in part; here they are not. I submit too that it shows that the tax on many things that are so necessary in the home is not and cannot be justified.
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker
I should like to refer to some of the effects of this heavy taxation. Taxation in excess of requirements is an added factor contributing to the increased cost of living. We have the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) in legislation to be introduced trying to find out ways and means of keeping down the cost of living, and other ministers in the government putting on additional taxation and doing their part thereby to raise the cost of living.
Governments are no different from individuals and when they have a lot of money lying around they consider it an invitation to spend. The non-defence expenditures which the Minister of Finance promised last spring would be reduced to a minimum have been increased and not decreased. The Minister of Finance has repeatedly stated that there was no need of a committee of parliament to be set up to cut down non-defence expenditures; that the government was doing their best; that they had committees and the treasury board and the like; that they had saved on civilian defence expenditures one and three-fifths cents on the dollar. Making allowance *'or additional provincial subsidies of $7-2 million; additional family allowances of $6-3 million; government contributions to the unemployment insurance fund of $2-8 million; old age and blind pensions, $3-6 million; general health grants, $4-2 million; not taking these into account at all we find that during seven months the ordinary non-defence expenditures in Canada have increased by $13-6 million, and this in spite of the promises by the government that in order to fight inflationary pressures civil expenditures would be kept down.
Another effect of high taxation has been increased lawlessness in this country. There is no greater invitation to lawlessness than unjustifiably high taxation in a nation which lies alongside another nation in which the same high taxation is not imposed. The tax on cigarettes in Canada is $11.50 per thousand or 23 cents per package of 20; in the United States it is 8 cents per package of 20, or $4 per thousand. Our tax on manufactured tobacco is $1.15 per pound and the United States tax is only 10 cents. On raw leaf the tax is 40 cents per pound in the United States and 10 cents per pound here. Tobacco products in Canada are subject to an additional federal sales tax of 10 per cent which is calculated on the total manufacturer's price. The cigarette tax at its present level is a detriment to the production of tobacco. It strikes a challenge to the existence of the tobacco farmers of this country and is an encouragement to the development of widespread contempt for the law. At the same time it has resulted in a loss of revenue to the country. Nobody has benefited by this
1724

The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker high tax, least of all the Canadian people or the revenues of this country. No amount of government stubbornness can justify its continuance. I am not going into the facts regarding the extent of the smuggling except to point out that in the Globe and Mail of December 4 there was an article in which, a high ranking mounted police officer was quoted as saying:
. . . enforcement is impossible. Seizures were made from time to time . . . but even fines and the loss of trucks did not stop the smugglers. No individual could stand the losses, and the fact that men whose trucks had been seized appeared again a short time later indicated the smuggling was operated by a well-financed ring.
Cigarette smuggling-and I have heard something about it in the last few days-has become a national scandal with up to 50 million United States cigarettes being brought into Canada each month according to the estimates of qualified people. The increase in taxation last spring was estimated to produce greater revenue to the extent of $26 million by the end of the year but has resulted in a loss of $20 million to the revenues of Canada.
Someone has argued in justification of the high tax that in England the tax is higher on tobacco and cigarettes. That is true, but there they do not have thousands of miles of border. Cigarette bootlegging is now big business. What is happening teaches the lesson that taxation can be made so high that revenues fall. Taxation can be raised so high, as it has been unjustifiably in the last few months, as to impede and interfere with production. Time magazine sums it up in these words:
The flood, estimated at 50 million cigarettes a month, continues unabated. The price is too good, the demand too great, the border too long and too free.
This menace, this undermining of the law will continue as long as taxation remains at its present height. I suggest that the only way in which excessive government spending can be stopped-and I am not going into the examples I have here today-is to keep the tax collectors poor, and not allow them to have more than is necessary within reasonable limits of expenditure. I think the time has come to say to the government: You must do away with unnecessary taxation and give the Canadian people a break. Remove the sales tax on necessities such as household appliances, clothing, prepared foods and the like in order that a contribution may be made by the government to a reduction in the cost of living. Unless we are to encourage smuggling over the next few months, and in spite of the minister having said a day or so ago in Montreal that he did not intend to do anything regarding taxation reduction at the present session, the time has come to make
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
provision for the immediate removal of the additional taxation imposed on cigarettes and tobacco at the last session. Second, after securing the approval of the governor in council the government should ask parliament to reduce unnecessarily high taxation, in the form of the sales tax on necessities, to levels consistent with requirements for government expenditures.
I shall now refer to an example of the kind of thing that arouses the Canadian people. The government is spending with almost profligate ease, taking from the Canadian people hundreds of millions of dollars more than are necessary; but what solicitude over a citizen in Manitoba who owed the government $5.76. I am sorry the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) is not here. Last Friday week the court of appeal of Manitoba brought down a judgment. It is one that governments can read with profit to themselves. This citizen's name is William Wood. On October 14, 1950, a letter was sent to him by the unemployment insurance commission stating that he owed $5.76 in insurance stamps, and twenty-four hours was given him within which to make up this terrible depredation at the expense of the Canadian people. He paid within twenty-four hours. On February 19, 1951, a charge was laid against him for not having paid the amount when he should have paid it. It was tried before the police magistrate on March 30, 1951, who dismissed the charge. Would you not have thought that was far enough to drag an honest taxpayer along the way of litigation?
The crown took him to the county court on an appeal and the hearing was held some months later. The county court judge dismissed the appeal. I do not want to mention this out of respect for the profession, but the Minister of Justice employed lawyers on the case, and against a man who dared to owe the Canadian people $5.76. The appeal was dismissed. Was the department satisfied? They went to the appeal division of the high court of Manitoba, and when you get into the high court, costs do mount. Last Friday week the court of appeal of Manitoba handed down its judgment dismissing the appeal. Mr. Justice Adamson and Mr. Justice Montague were in favour of dismissing it while Mr. Justice Coyne dissented. Mr. Justice Adamson said that the county court judge was correct in dismissing the appeal. Referring to the letter as a result of which Mr. Wood paid the $5.76 within twenty-four hours, Mr. Justice Adamson said:
That letter and the immediate compliance . . . should have been taken as settling the matter. That is what any reasonable or fair person would have considered the letter meant. However, the complainant Rudd, on behalf of the commission, then

laid this charge and has seen fit to press it through three courts. The respondent has remedied his fault-he owes no money. The charge was purely technical . . .
Apparently there is a threat that the crown is going to carry the case to the Supreme Court of Canada because, Mr. Speaker, there is some principle at stake. I ask that the responsible minister put an end once and for all to this nonsense of treating a taxpayer in this way who remedied his default within twenty-four hours; and that is what the court of appeal said. Mr. Justice Coyne, who dissented, said:
Further litigation would be still more unfortunate and not conducive to justice.
However, he said in his dissent that he felt the man had done wrong and he would have imposed a fine of $1 without costs. The court by a majority dismissed the case. When, on the one hand, you see a government unjustifiably spending-and I could mention examples of recent months, but I am not going to because there will be another opportunity to deal with the question of overexpenditure and unjustifiable expenditure- you understand why the Winnipeg Tribune on Monday last had an editorial entitled "Poor show by Ottawa Brass". The editorial reads in part:
What we would like to know and what a lot of people would like to know is how much these three trials cost the commission in court costs and lawyers' fees.
I think it would be most interesting to ascertain what was the amount of that wasteful expenditure.
I am asking the government at this present session to end this national scandal of cigarette smuggling that is taking place and that is resulting in law-breaking by thousands, while at the same time the little fellow in Manitoba for $5.76, which he paid when notified, is dragged through three courts in order to maintain the dignity of the law. If the dignity of the law is to be maintained for $5.76, there are immeasurably greater reasons for assuring the maintenance of the dignity of the law of this country by enacting legislation at this session to remove the extra tobacco taxes that have caused wholesale bootlegging and law-breaking. By doing so the house will be actually increasing the revenues of the Minister of Finance for the next several months of the fiscal year. At the same time, if parliament removes the sales tax in so far as necessities are concerned and the surtax on income tax, it will be doing something to restore equilibrium between what the actual costs of running government and defence will be and the amount of taxes that should be taken from the Canadian people.
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), that the following words be added to the amendment:
And further regrets that Your Excellency's advisers continue to collect unnecessarily high taxes beyond requirements and have failed at the present session of parliament to relieve the people from unnecessary, burdensome and unjustified taxation.

speechtext:
The question I must determine is whether the amendment moved by the hon. member for Lake Centre is in order. It is necessary that an amendment which is moved at this time should be relevant to the amendment as amended. I am not sure that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Lake Centre is relevant to that amendment. I am not making a ruling in advance, but it seems to me that it might be more appropriate if this amendment were moved when the main motion as amended is presented to the house. I shall be glad to hear hon. members on it.	;
However, perhaps we might consider it from a practical point of view. May I just for a moment do something that is probably a little unusual, and refer to the ruling which I made last Wednesday on the amendment which was moved by the hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Bater). Hon. members will recall that in making my ruling at that time, I said I had had very little time to study the precedents. I did refer to the fact that I could find only one instance in which a similar amendment had been moved. The other day, when I was reading Beauchesne's third edition, I ran across a ruling which was made by Mr. Speaker Lemieux on June 26, 1926. I find that a similar amendment was moved at that time. It is interesting to note that the amendment which was moved at that time, and which struck out all the effective words of the amendment which was then standing, was moved by Mr. Woodsworth, who at that time represented the riding of Winnipeg North Centre. Apparently it has been characteristic of the people of that riding to send to parliament men who have a very keen appreciation of the rules of this house. I recall that last Wednesday the present member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) argued against the regularity of the subamendment. I would like him to read the amendment which was moved in 1926.
On Wednesday of last week it was said that hon. members might not have an opportunity of voting on the subamendment which was then before the house; but if members will read the words of the Speaker which appear on page 629 of Beauchesne's third edition they will see that he also considered that question,

The Address-Mr. Abbott
Since my ruling of last week was an important one, with the permission of the house may I refer in this debate to my ruling of last Wednesday, that is, to correct my ruling by referring to the debate that took place in 1926. I think it might be helpful on some future occasion.

speechtext: I must dispose of the present amendment which has been moved by the hon. member for Lake Centre. Probably it should be moved, to be in order, on the main motion as amended. Probably it would save the time of the house, without this being considered a precedent, if the amendment of the hon. member for Lake Centre were allowed to stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly have no quarrel with your ruling on the procedural matter. I had not given it any consideration myself. Whatever the strict legality of the matter may be, I agree with the views you have expressed that it might be well to dispose of the question now. I have not had occasion to speak to the house for some little time. In view of a good deal of what the hon. member for Lake Centre has said, it would seem that this is perhaps an appropriate opportunity to do so. I appreciate his courtesy in withholding the comments which he had to make today until I could again be in the house.
He has raised some very important questions, raised them with his usual force and vigour. They are questions which merit a reply, and that reply I intend to give this afternoon.
At the outset let me hasten to state the obvious. It is clear, of course, that the revenues which have been accruing to the treasury during the first seven months of the year are substantially in excess of those which I estimated when I delivered my budget speech last spring. It is clear also that expenditures, particularly in defence, are not running at the full rate which was contemplated at that time. Nevertheless, the criticism which has appeared with respect to the surplus which is accruing, and the alleged overtaxation, implies necessarily that in submitting these estimates last April I must have been either dishonest or incompetent. I concede readily that the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) would not suggest for a moment that I possess the

first of these qualities, and I doubt whether he would press very hard the second one. Nevertheless I think that is the necessary implication of the charges that have been made in some other places.
Let me say this at the outset, Mr. Speaker. In the estimates I have placed before the house in the five years that I have been Minister of Finance, every estimate has been made with complete honesty, without mental reservations, and based upon the best technical advise available to me, either within or outside the government service. Moreover, I have made a practice of disclosing fully and frankly in my budget speech, and in the accompanying papers, the basis of my statistical estimates. In every budget I have explained and emphasized the difficulties of forecasting. I do -not need to tell the house again, because I have done it before, that estimates of expenditures have to be forecast some fifteen to eighteen months before the end of the year to which they refer. Right now we are, of course, in the middle of preparing and compiling our estimates for the coming fiscal year which will end on March 31, 1953.
On the revenue side, the Minister of Finance brings down his forecast of revenue in March or April. As a rule these forecasts are based on statistics, the latest of which are available for January or February, and many of them are still only preliminary estimates for December. So that as a consequence the forecast of revenue must look fourteen or fifteen months ahead. These forecasts are all subject to a change in price levels, shifts in imports and exports, the ups and downs of employment and investment, and other unforeseen changes in the economic climate both at home and abroad.
If hon. members will cast their minds back they will recall that almost every year, far from being charged with being too pessimistic in my forecasts, I have been charged with being too optimistic. I well remember that as late as March 1950 my hon. friend the financial critic of the opposition, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) charged me with being unduly optimistic. He pointed out that a small change in my estimates for that year, a small change in business conditions, could result in a deficit rather than a surplus. On the average, over the past four years, performance has exceeded forecast by just about 12 per cent. My revenues, over this period- of unprecedented prosperity in the history of Canada, have on the average exceeded expenditures by about 12 per cent. Expenditures are much more easily forecast because they are more directly under our control than- are revenues. In the past four years actual results have exceeded

forecasts by only about 4 per cent. All governments at all levels have been faced with these same difficulties, and I have been far from alone in underestimating revenues during the period to which I refer. In the fiscal years ending in 1951 actual revenues exceeded forecasts in the case of some provincial and other governments as follows: Ontario, 16 per cent; Quebec, 19 per cent; British Columbia, 17 per cent; Alberta, 40 per cent; United States, 29 per cent. This is against the average which I mentioned in the case of federal revenues of approximately 12 per cent.	,
As the hon. member for Lake Centre has pointed out, this year I forecast our revenues at $3,730 million. I told the house explicitly that this was based on the following assumptions: First, high employment; second, average crops; third, a price level not much higher than in April; fourth, gross national production of $20 billion. In my budget speech I went on to say that should production and incomes continue to rise beyond that level- as they well might-I should expect my forecast to be exceeded. Should they not go quite that high, our revenues could fall short of the estimates I was submitting. This figure of $20 billion was based on careful studies prepared by experts in the Department of Trade and Commerce, and it compared with a gross national product the preceding year of $17-5 billion. In other words, it assumed an increase during the coming year of 12 per cent over 1950, as compared with increases of 6 per cent and 8 per cent respectively in the two preceding years.
I said that of that estimated 12 per cent increase in gross production, about half was estimated to be in price increase and about half in volume. It now seems reasonably certain that our 1951 gross national production will be something over $21 billion, or an increase of about 18 per cent. In other words, it is about 6 per cent higher than I forecast. There have been greater increases in both price and volume than either my officials or I expected, or that any other responsible person could have estimated. I would not have believed it possible we could continue to increase our gross national production at the rate we have during the past four or five years. Therefore, unless there are other unforeseen changes-which I do not expect-I anticipate that our revenues next March 31 will exceed my forecast by about 8 per cent or 9 per cent, or by some $300 million to $350 million.
As I have said, normally our expenditures are much easier to forecast accurately, but this year there have been some unusual problems.
The Address-Mr. Abbott Apart from defence, and the new universal old age pension payments which will start on January 1, it looks as though our expenditures will exceed our forecasts, but only by 3 per cent or 4 per cent, and this in spite of higher construction costs than I had expected, and the further increases in salaries and in the pay of armed forces and the R.C.M.P. which will be announced shortly. Hon. members will do well to recall, in comparing last year's expenditures with this year's expenditures, that government costs have increased in the same ways other costs have increased. If you take into account these factors and the increases in the salaries and wages, and government services, it would have been a fairly creditable achievement to have held our non-defence expenditures at the level of last year. In fact, that would mean an appreciable reduction in government services.
As to defence expenditures, the actual expenditures on defence for the year which will end on March 31 were most difficult to forecast. A year ago at this time, when the armed services were presenting their estimates to the members of the treasury board, they honestly thought they could usefully spend a good deal more than the $1-7 billion which parliament voted. So far as we were concerned, it was not a disagreement on needs or speed. It was a matter of judgment as to how much could be procured or constructed in that twelve-month period. As the house knows, the final amount which was voted by parliament for defence was approximately $1-7 billion.
To my personal knowledge every country is finding it most difficult, almost impossible, to carry through its planned defence program at the planned rate; and we are certainly no exception to that general rule. Those parts of our program which are wholly within our own control are well up to schedule, but such matters as construction, which depends on imported steel or imported equipment, and on equipment and supplies which must be procured in the United States or elsewhere, either in finished form or in the form of key components, are behind schedule. The services hope, of course, that they can catch up a good part of that lag before March 31, but it is clear to me now that the defence votes which parliament appropriated last year will most certainly not be fully spent before the end of this year, although commitments will have been incurred which will fall due for payment in coming fiscal periods.
In saying that we have been delayed by inability to obtain certain essential supplies from outside, I am not casting any criticism,

The Address-Mr. Abbott of course, on the United States or on any other country from which we have to obtain these materials. It is a common problem, one which is shared by all of us. We have to take our place in the agreed production schedule, and having regard to the world situation we cannot always claim first priority.
What is this surplus that we have heard so much talk about?) I must confess that I have been somewhat surprised at what seemed to me to be the rather naive and erroneous inferences drawn from our monthly statements by people who really ought to know better. The monthly statements of the comptroller are, of course, completely accurate summaries of each month's revenues and expenditures. But surely all hon. members know better than to take one or three or six months' figures and multiply by 12 or 4 or 2. A most elementary checking back on published figures would save people from some of these erroneous inferences.
Revenues, of course, come in fairly evenly throughout the year, since income taxes were placed on a pay-as-you-earn basis. There is normally a slight slump in the summer and a moderate peak in the final quarter of the fiscal year. But expenditures are highly irregular and they have a pronounced seasonal pattern. They do not occur in a regular 8 per cent a month or a regular 25 per cent a quarter. The house will be interested to know that the past three fiscal years show the following average quarterly pattern:
April to June, 17 per cent of total annual expenditure.
July to September, 21 per cent of total annual expenditure.
In other words, approximately one-third of your total expenditures come in the first six months of the year.
October to December, 22 per cent of total annual expenditure.
January to March, 40 per cent of total annual expenditure.
The low figure for the first quarter and the very high figure for the last quarter show perhaps the most conspicuous feature of that pattern. That is due to two long established accounting practices in the government service.
By statute all payments actually made in April on account of expenditures properly incurred prior to March 31 are charged back into March. That means that the comptroller's figure for April budgetary expenditures covers barely half a normal month, while his March figure is, as a rule, about double a normal or average month.

The second point is that the whole of certain large annual expenditures such as deficits on government-operated railways and the like, government contributions to the superannuation fund, interest on numerous trust funds and the like, and on post office savings accounts, reserve against active assets and these other items are charged at the end of the fiscal year. The net effect of these two practices is that the month of March normally shows expenditures which are equal to those of any three other months.
All these figures are available from the comptroller's monthly statements and from tables which are in the public accounts.
If the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) will take the trouble to refer to page 18 of the public accounts for 1951, for example, he will see that last year our October month-end surplus was $363 million, that the peak month-end surplus rose to $649 million in January, but that our final surplus was $211 million. So that if I did not have a fairly substantial surplus by the end of October or November, it would be quite clear that I would be bound to run into a substantial deficit at the end of the fiscal year.
As the house is well aware, our accumulated budgetary surplus for the first seven months of this year stood at approximately $605 million, compared with 1 $363 million at the same period last year. That does not mean, of course, that we have on hand an extra $605 million in cash because, in addition to our ordinary or budgetary expenditures, we have had to lay out the following funds:
Millions
Loans to or investments in housing, railways, farm loans, foreign exchange reserves, etc	 $293
Cost of replacing defence equipment supplied from stock to NATO countries	 74
The house will recall when we transferred existing equipment to some of our allies in NATO, we set up a credit in a special account for the value of that equipment and that can be drawn against to purchase new equipment, but that represented a cash outgo but is not reflected as a disbursement in our books in the year in which the cash is paid out. The other items are:
Millions
Redemption of international bank demand
notes	 $ 7
Net reduction in matured debt	 16
Redemptions of Canada savings bonds and of war savings certificates	 131
Total	 $521
After taking care of these obligations we have left only $84 million out of our $605 million budgetary surplus.

We also have non-revenue cash receipts, such as purchases of annuities, deposits in post office savings accounts, loan repayments by other governments and so on, amounting in all to about $124 million, so that our actual cash on October 31 was $208 million above April 1.
Perhaps I might add here that during November we paid off $523 million of debt, but we borrowed $492 million, largely Canada savings bonds which were the only new borrowing during that period, or a further net use of cash of $31 million to reduce debt.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What were the securities paid off?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I have not the figures here now, -but they are readily available. As anyone who is familiar with conditions as they exist today knows, as things have turned out in New York, in London, as well as in Canada, we can congratulate ourselves, I think, that we have had a substantial surplus so far for this year; because if we had not had a surplus we would have been obliged to borrow additional new money to the tune of $300 million to finance housing, the C.N.R., and other government loans and investments, and another $200 million to meet maturing debt, or $500 million in all.
Those who know something about the bond market will realize that the marketing of an additional $500 million of new bonds during recent months would have had to take one or the other of two forms. Since there is no pool of idle savings in Canada, the sale of $500 million of Canadian federal government securities would have diverted an equivalent amount of savings away from private investment in housing, in municipal improvements, in hydro, or in oil or iron developments and the like. If there had been that much less private capital investment, obviously we would have had less employment, less imports, less revenue and a much smaller budgetary surplus. That would have been one way to get $500 million.
Alternatively we could have borrowed $500 million from the banking system. But that would have been straight inflationary financing under existing conditions; and I well remember the strong disapproval voiced by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) in August of last year when, for good and sufficient reasons, we temporarily financed a $200 million inflow of United States funds by borrowing $200 million from the banks.
So that our current surplus has been, in part, a reflection of inflationary pressure. But had we had no surplus the effects of those
The Address-Mr. Abbott
pressures on price levels would have been very much more startling than they have been.
Those who may have taken the trouble to examine the details of the public accounts will have noticed that there have been only two successions of years since confederation when we have significantly reduced our public debt. The first was after world war I, in the period 1923-29, when during most of that time my predecessor Mr. Robb was minister of finance. We had a succession of surpluses during those years totalling $276 million. Those surpluses equalled about 10 per cent of our revenue in those years, and during that period of time we reduced our debt by about 11 per cent from its -peak.
The second period during which we have reduced our debt has been the years commencing with 1947, since your humble servant has been Minister of Finance. In those five years we have had surpluses averaging about $375 million a year, or about 13 per cent of our revenue in those years. Those were the most prosperous years in Canada's history, and if one is ever to achieve any reduction in the national debt, then surely it is wise to do so during a period of prosperity.
As a matter of fact, as of last March we had reduced our net debt by about $2 billion or approximately 15 per cent, during the period to which I have referred. The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) has referred to existing taxation, and made reference in particular to the additional taxes imposed on tobacco. I am not going to deal in detail with the various suggestions he has made concerning reductions in this tax. I wish to say this, that as a general rule I think it is desirable that tax changes should be made once a year. It is extremely embarrassing for the business community to be in a period of uncertainty, wondering whether commodity taxes in particular are going to go off or go on at varying periods of the year. I departed from that principle on two occasions, one of which was at the beginning of the war in Korea and the second when we dissolved prior to the passing of a budget. But, speaking generally and referring to the general principle, I think it is undesirable that tax changes should be made more often than once a year, and I have no intention of recommending any changes in the tax structure until the budget presentation next spring.
The tobacco tax is a tax imposed for revenue. It is not imposed to prevent people from smoking. My hon. friend has rightly pointed out that, in respect of commodity taxes, as in other things, one can run into the law of diminishing return. The question of the tobacco tax, as in the case of all other taxes, will be considered between now and the

The Address-Mr. Knowles
presentation of the budget next spring. If it is desirable at that time to make any change, that change will be made. But I would caution hon. members against jumping to too quick conclusions about the effect of the additional tax. Unquestionably the consumption of cigarettes in particular is down. That Is probably due in part to the increase in tax, In part to the increase in price made by the manufacturers of cigarettes, and in part to the accumulation of inventories prior to the budget, both because it was felt that the tax might be raised, as indeed was the case, and also because in the case of one large producer labour troubles were anticipated and later developed.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: And smuggling.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The question of smuggling is a very important one. I agree with the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) that when a tax or any other impost is pushed to the point where there is too great an incentive to break the law, then that situation should be pretty carefully considered. I can assure him and other hon. members that, between now and budget time, revenue officials will do their best to see that smuggling is kept down to a minimum.
That is the picture. I have nothing for which to apologize in my budget of last year. I have said fully and frankly that revenues have exceeded my expectations. But in the light of the responsibilities we have before us, and in the light of the inflationary pressures which exist today, I take pride in the results which have been achieved. And so far as I am concerned I am quite prepared to leave the verdict to time.
If one travels outside Canada, as I and a good many hon. members have, I am sure they will find, as I did, that Canada's record in the fiscal and economic sphere is considered as one which, without indulging in any overstatement, compares very favourably with that of any other country. Therefore, I deny, Mr. Speaker, that there has been any overtaxation of the Canadian people, and I am quite prepared to stand by the fiscal proposals I made last April. When next March or April comes we will see then what has to be done.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I comment on the new subamendment, and before I make reference to a further matter which I wish to discuss, perhaps I might be permitted to offer a comment on the position you have taken, sir, with respect to the subamendment of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). As I listened to you it seemed to me that you said quite clearly two things. In the first place, you expressed the view that this subamendment would have been more in
order as an amendment to the main motion as amended, when we reach that stage. With that I fully agree. But you also expressed the view that since the same practical result is obtained by deciding now whether or not this additional regret is to be added, it might be just as well for the house to give its decision now on the substance of the matter, rather than to have a long debate on procedure.
I agree with your judgment and your wisdom in that matter; and I offer as evidence in support of the position you have taken the fact that the record of the decision to which you called the attention of the house, namely that of Mr. Speaker Lemieux on June 26, 1926, occupies twenty full pages in Beau-chesne's third edition. That is to say, it took twenty pages to record the important parts of the debate on that point of order and the Speaker's decision. In other words, had we at this time got into a debate as to the propriety or otherwise of the subamendment, we might have had to amend the hours of sitting still further in order to finish this session's business before Christmas.
Perhaps while I am saying a word about this decision I might point out that although we were interested in your reference to Mr. Woodsworth, the point of order did not relate to Mr. Woodsworth's subamendment itself. Mr. Woodsworth's subamendment to Mr. Stevens' amendment apparently was not questioned but was defeated by a vote of 117 to 115. Then there was a subamendment by Mr. Fansher which carried, and then there was a later attempt to move another subamendment at a point corresponding to the point, at which we now find ourselves. That was made by Mr. Rinfret and a long procedural argument developed. Mr. Speaker Lemieux finally ruled in favour of Mr. Rinfret's subamendment. So far, that would seem to indicate that there might be propriety in the subamendment being moved at this time.
On the other hand, and this is rather unique, in Beauchesne's third edition at page 630 we find in small print at the end of that long recital a letter to Dr. Beauchesne written by T. Lonsdale Webster, who was then Clerk of the British House of Commons. This was in reply to an inquiry which it appears Dr. Beauchesne had sent to Mr. Webster, and it would seem from Mr. Webster's reply that he had some doubt about Mr. Speaker Lemieux's ruling. 1 note with interest the last sentence of Mr. Webster's letter, which reads:
So far as Mr. Rinfret differed from Mr. Woodsworth, he should, I think, have moved amendments by way of additions to Mr. Stevens' amendment when that amendment became the substantive question.

I shall not add to the confusion, as I think I have demonstrated my point with these few references. Had Your Honour decided to entertain a procedural debate as to whether or not this subamendment is in order at this time we would have been here for quite a while. After all, at some point or other, either now or later, an amendment of this kind would be in order, and I think it is well that the house be given an opportunity to decide on the substance of the amendment which has been moved by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker), and that is what you, sir, have done.
I listened with interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Lake Centre and I listened also with interest and attention to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) when he tried to answer the charge, both in the hon. member's speech and in the amendment, that there is unnecessary taxation in this country at the present time. Despite all the figures he produced, despite the reference to the way in which money comes in at one time of the year more heavily than at another, frankly I could not see that the Minister of Finance was able to offset the fact that the present rates of taxation are taking from the Canadian people sums of money greatly in excess of what is really needed, and at a time when our people are having an exceedingly difficult time to meet the still rising cost of living.
At the end of his remarks the Minister of Finance indicated what he believed to be the principle to be followed in matters of taxation. If I heard him correctly he said he believed that as a general rule there should be tax changes only once a year. I want to say that the Minister of Finance and the government have another rule regarding tax changes. That rule is that there are to be tax reductions only once a parliament, and the time for those tax reductions is just before an election.
The Minister of Finance referred to this himself when he gave the exceptions to the rule of making tax changes only once a year. He said there had been two occasions when he had broken that rule, one being when taxes were increased because of the situation in Korea and the other, as he put it, in that interesting year of 1949 when parliament was dissolved before the budget was adopted. For a few years prior to 1949 the practice was to build up surpluses. That was part of the government's theory of cyclical budgeting. Suddenly when we were on the eve of an election that theory was thrown out the 94699-111
The Address-Mr. Knowles window and it was considered desirable to give the Canadian people substantial reductions in taxation just before an election.
We are back in the same cycle again. It would be interesting to find out just what point in the cycle we have reached. The government is still building up surpluses. Of course nothing is more risky in the political field than to make predictions, but I shall make the prediction that these surpluses will continue to mount until the eve of the next election. On the eve of the next election these surpluses will be used to bring about reductions in taxation.
When the minister brings down his budget in March or April of next spring, if there are substantial tax reductions because of this huge surplus to which attention has been drawn we will all know what it means. It will mean an election in June, 1952. If next year the Minister of Finance in his budget speech continues to assert his belief in the desirability of draining off these surpluses so as to pay off more of the national debt, we will know that the election is not yet.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

It will be very interesting to see what happens, but I believe the rule will hold so far as this government is concerned, that taxation changes should be made only once a year and taxation reductions are to be made only once a parliament, and that just before a general election.
The subject about which I wish to have something to say at this time is not unrelated to the fact that the government has quite a pool of money on hand just now, but it is a little different in nature. I refer to the plight of the retired pensioners of Canadian National Railways. This is a matter which some of us have raised on several occasions this session by means of questions on the orders of the day. We have asked whether the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) would soon be in a position to announce general changes in the pension structure of Canadian National Railways. In particular we have asked whether there would be any increase in the pensions of Canadian National employees already retired.
Thus far the only answer we have been able to get from the Minister of Transport is to the effect that he has not yet been advised as to what is the situation, but when he does get that information he will communicate it to the house. Let me read the answer he gave on one occasion which in substance is the same as the answer he has given every time. When the minister was

The Address-Mr. Knowles replying to a question of mine on November 15 he said, as reported on page 1044 of Hansard:
I can only reply to that, as has already been stated in the house, that Canadian National Railways pension rules are now under reconsideration, and my understanding is that the brotherhoods and the railways are discussing changes in the pension rules. I have not been advised what they are; but when I am, I should be in a postiion to give information to the house.
I emphasize the word "information". That is what the Minister of Transport has indicated he might be in position to give to the house this session. Information is sufficient if it is the right information, but I wish to point out that in my view the responsibility of the Minister of Transport and of the government goes further than the desirability of imparting information to this house.
I base that claim on certain statements that were made at the last session of parliament by the minister. He and others will remember that we had quite a series of debates here and elsewhere on the question of Canadian National pensions during the last session of parliament. Those in the house who took part in that debate were the Minister of Transport, on the government side, and the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) and I in the main on this side of the house. In addition to the discussions we had in the house there was a discussion of the whole question in the special committee on railways and shipping owned, operated and controlled by the government. One of the features of the discussion in the committee, and later in the house, was a certain letter which had been addressed jointly to the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) and myself by a trade union official on behalf of some of the interested employees. Copies of that letter were sent to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) and to the president of the Canadian National Railways. It was thought by them that the letter was a suggestion to us that we should not be pressing this matter too much in parliament. I want to come back to that in a moment. I point out to the minister and to others that I now have before me a copy of a further letter written by the same Mr. A. A. Hutchinson, who is general chairman of the order of railroad telegraphers, urging the Canadian National employees affected to get in touch with their members of parliament and to get them to put pressure upon the government here in the house.
