speechtext: What is the date of that letter?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The date of this letter is October 3, 1951. It is included in a mimeographed circular letter sent out by the general chairman of the brotherhood of railroad trainmen. It is a very interesting letter of three full pages which goes into the whole question of what is likely to happen with respect to Canadian National pensions. In the letter Mr. Hutchinson says, in reply to retired C.N.R. pensioners who are pleading for some adjustment of their position, that there was a meeting of the vice-presidents with the general chairmen and that certain recommendations were made to the C.N.R. board of directors which were considered at their January meeting. Then he says:
We have no official information as to what was recommended but unofficially we do understand that the board did make certain recommendations in regard to changes which would have been beneficial and these recommendations were submitted to the Hon. Mr. Chevrier, Minister of Transport, for government approval.
Then there is another paragraph comparing the position of the Canadian Pacific Railway with its responsibility to its shareholders and that of Canadian National Railways with its responsibility to parliament. Then there follows this paragraph:
We understand that the government refused to give approval to the recommendation of the board of directors and gave as the reason that "it would be contrary to declared public policy" as set out in a press release dated January 23, 1948 . . .
And so on. At the last session the Minister of Transport and the president of Canadian National Railways accepted Mr. Hutchinson as an unqualified authority, and I did not object to their doing so. The point I wish to make at this juncture is that it appears from Mr. Hutchinson's letter, which, as I say, is being widely circulated amongst Canadian National retired employees who are concerned about their plight, that the Canadian National board of directors did make a recommendation that something be done with respect to the plight of retired C.N.R. pensioners. But it is also clear from Mr. Hutchinson's letter that so far as they can ascertain the recommendation made by the C.N.R. board of directors was turned down by the government.
Therefore, as I said a few moments ago, the Minister of Transport and the government have a greater responsibility than merely that of imparting information to this house. The minister is not just an errand boy to tell us what the Canadian National has decided. The minister is the person who, with his colleagues in the government, makes the final decision as to whether or not anything is to be done on behalf of retired C.N.R. employees. I remind the Minister of Transport that he took that position in the house

last April 27 when we were debating this whole question. I am looking at page 2459 of Hansard for that date, and I note that he said:
This is first and foremost a matter for Canadian National Railways and its employees to decide, and that is exactly what Mr. Hutchinson says. That is exactly as it should be, because parliament has authorized the Canadian National Railways management to deal with problems such as this.
I agree it is first and foremost a C.N.R. matter, to be settled with the employees, but the Minister of Transport went on to say:
But if it turns out that they are unable to deal with their employees and they make representations to the government with reference to the matters to which my hon. friends have referred, then I think it is not only the duty but the responsibility of the government to decide whether or not it will revise upwards or take no action with reference to this problem. Therefore I say, putting it in its proper light, that this is a matter which is now under discussion between the authorities of the Canadian National Railways and its employees. It is being given careful consideration by a joint committee of the employees and the officers. I think, as the letter states, we should at least give the committee a chance to see what it is possible to do. If they are not successful in dealing with it, then I think it will be the responsibility of the government if Canadian National Railways should decide to recommend to the government a plan upon which both will have agreed, or an alternative plan in case both cannot agree.
I agree with the position the minister took last April, namely, that the people to deal with this matter first of all are the railways on the one hand and the employees on the other. But the minister also said last April that if the railways come forward with a recommendation it is the government's responsibility to decide what to do with it. He also said if the railways and the employees cannot get together then it is the government's responsibility to make up its mind what is to be done in that situation. The reference of the Minister of Transport to a letter in the quotation I have just read is a reference to the letter from Mr. Hutchinson who at that time took the view that at that stage of the game this was a matter to be worked out between the employees and the company.
Now Mr. Hutchinson says in the further letter to which I have referred that the information which has come to them is that, whatever may be done with regard to changes in the basic plan, there is nothing in prospect by way of any increase or adjustment for C.N.R. employees who are already retired. Mr. Hutchinson says that in a further paragraph in his latest letter:
We have been and still are proceeding to revise the pension rules and expect to have a new set of rules to put into effect soon, probably January 1, 1952, but these new rules will only apply to future pensions and will do nothing for those who go on pension before they take effect.
94699-llli
The Address-Mr. Knowles
The same Mr. Hutchinson who was quoted by the minister and the president last April sees what these retired employees are up against, and he goes on to say:
I feel quite sure that if C.N.R. pensioners are to get any consideration, other than that which is being given generally under bill 395-
That was last session's old age assistance bill.
-that such consideration must be given by the government of Canada in its role as shareholder of the Canadian National Railways, and if your veterans associations are to accomplish any good I believe you will have to work through members of parliament who have influence with the government rather than through C.N.R. officials who do not seem to be able to apply their wishes to the problem. If the general chairmen's association can be of assistance we will be glad to do so but about all we could do would be to add the weight of our appeal to the members of parliament to your own appeals, as our appeals to the C.N.R. on your behalf have met with failure on account of government opposition.
That letter is signed by A. A. Hutchinson, representing the general chairmen's association in respect of pension matters. Mr. Hutchinson was regarded at the? last session, I thought erroneously, as the government's chief witness in this whole matter. I regarded him as our witness, and now the matter is clear. There is the way Mr. Hutchinson now sees the position. He affirms that something should be done with regard to the basic pension plan so far as those still in the service are concerned. But, he says: "Despite our best efforts we could get nowhere by way of getting any changes for those who are already retired. We thought we had made headway with the board of directors, but that board has run into government opposition and so the only way you are going to get anywhere by way of any change is by persuading the government that something should be done for those men who are already retired". It is for that reason, Mr. Speaker, before this debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne comes to an end, I feel that I want to put this matter squarely up to the government and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier). I regret that the minister is not in his place. No doubt he is engaged in something that prevents him from being here. Just for the record I want to say that I did send him a note about an hour ago to the effect that I intended to raise this matter if I was able to get the floor. Nevertheless I hope that he will read these remarks and that he will take them into consideration. I have noted his positive statement across the floor of the house that as soon as he gets information as to what the Canadian National is going to do he will impart it to the house. Well, from Mr. Hutchinson's letter it would appear that that information is not going to be very helpful to those now retired. My fear is that

The Address-Mr. Knowles we will not get that report until a day or two after parliament has prorogued. That often happens with respect to statements that are unsatisfactory. After we have gone home, and can no longer say anything about it here, an announcement is made. I hope that will not happen this time. Let us have the announcement now.
I have put these figures on the record so often I certainly should not do it again in any detail; but in passing may I just refer to figures that were placed upon Hansard on March 12, 1951, at pages 1129 to 1131, respecting Canadian National pensions. These figures were given in answer to questions that I had placed on the order paper. Just to pick out a couple of examples, they show that as at that date last spring 3,256 Canadian National pensioners were drawing a pension of only $25 a month. They also show that a total of 7,269 pensioners of the Canadian National Railways were drawing a pension of less than $40 a month.
One of the suggestions that has been made frequently when this debate has come up is that these people would get some assistance, some improvement in their position, when the old age pension legislation was sorted out, including old age security for those 70 and over and old age assistance for those between 65 and 69. Well, the old age assistance provided for those between 65 and 69 is really of no help to these people who already have a little something. The means test is there, and these men who have even a small pension from the Canadian National Railways will in most cases be precluded by that small pension from drawing old age assistance. So far as old age security improving the pension position of those 70 and over is concerned, I want to say I do not think that the government, or any other employer in this country, public or private, should use the fact that there is old age security as an excuse for crawling out from under its responsibilities to its retired employees. This is a responsibility which still rests on the employers of these people. The employer is the Canadian National Railways which the people of Canada own, and which is administered under the direction of the parliament of Canada. These are our employees, and our responsibilities to them are such that I do not feel we can continue to allow 3,256 of them to draw as their industrial pension only $25 a month, nor can we allow 7,269 of them to draw pensions from the railways, for whom they have worked, of less than $40 a month. This is a question separate from old age pensions. It stands on its own feet, and I insist that the federal government has a responsibility to deal with it properly.


As I say, prior to the circulation of this last letter by Mr. Hutchinson, some of us had ideas as to what was happening; but we did not have the evidence in black and white. But now Mr. Hutchinson says it is quite clear what has happened. The Canadian National Railways was prepared to do something for its retired employees, those already on small pensions, but any recommendation they made, whatever it was, says Mr. Hutchinson of the general chairmen's association, has been turned down by the government. And says he, "We, your trade union representatives, in our efforts on behalf of the retired employees have run into government opposition." Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I have raised the matter here to put the responsibility clearly where it now belongs, namely on this government and on the Minister of Transport who must be responsible for any recommendations in this field. It is not good1 enough to leave those pensions at those figures. That basic pension should be increased. It should be certainly a good deal more than $25 a .month. Last spring when we were debating this I suggested it should be $40 a month. The cost of living has gone up since then. I would suggest that $50 a month is a more reasonable figure for that basic Canadian National Railways pension at this time, apart from the service pension and any other provisions. If a change in that basic pension could be made, on the understanding that it would apply to those who are now retired, it would be meeting to some extent at least the responsibility of the government to those people; and I make the plea as strongly as I can to the minister and the government that they deal with this matter right now.
It would seem from the terms of Mr. Hutchinson's letter that an announcement may be made before January 1, 1952, which is not very far away, concerning basic changes in the structure of Canadian National pensions. Mr. Speaker, I think it would be a tragedy and most unfortunate if, when that announcement is made, nothing is said as to the position and the plight of those already retired, and I plead with the government to deal with this matter now so that any announcement which is made will include both groups. Let there be improvements for those still in the service; that too is most important. But right now it is imperative that there be an increase for those who are retired already, particularly those in the lower brackets.
I wish to say a few words in that same vein with respect to retired civil servants. As hon. members know this, too, is a question which I have raised a good many times. It, too, is a question which the Minister of

Finance and others have said should wait until we have dealt with old age assistance and old age security. With respect to these retired employees I want to say the same thing I have said with respect to Canadian National employees, namely that it is not right for any employer, be he a private employer, the federal government or any other government, to crawl out from under its responsibility to pay proper pensions to its employees merely because the Old Age Assistance Act and the Old Age Security Act are now on the statute books of this country.
The last figures that I had with respect to retired civil servants are contained in sessional paper 102-C, which was tabled on March 12, 1951, in response to questions of mine which were made an order for return on Monday, February 19, 1951. This return gives a good many figures and a good many different brackets, but to pick out the significant ones I would point out that at that time-in March of this year-there were
9.877	retired federal civil servants. Of those
9.877	some 1,478 were receiving pensions of $39.99 a month or less. In addition there were 4,677 widows of retired civil servants drawing pensions provided by statute. Of those 4,677 considerably more than half, 2,647 to be exact, were drawing pensions of $39.99 a month or less. In other words, in both cases these are the numbers drawing pensions of less than $40 a month.
As hon. members and the Minister of Finance well know, this matter has been brought to their attention repeatedly. I have in my hand a copy of the correspondence exchanged recently between the association of superannuated civil servants at Toronto and the Minister of Finance. The letter to the minister contains a reference to the sympathy which the minister expressed for these people the last time a delegation met him, so the minister replied on October 11, 1951, that he still had that sympathy but he felt the retired civil servants should look for such improvement as they might want to the Old Age Assistance Act and the Old Age Security Act. Again, Mr. Speaker, we have here an example of an employer doing something which I believe is totally wrong, that is, crawling out from under his own responsibilities by virtue of a public statute.
I am sure that if the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) were to hear of any private employer doing anything like that because of the Old Age Security Act he would frown upon it. He would say that this pension, small enough as it is, is being given to everyone on a national basis, and does not take the place of the responsibility of a private employer. I suggest that that applies to the
The Address-Mr. Applewhaite federal government as well. It is not good enough to tell these faithful servants of the federal government who are on these low pensions that the only supplement they can have is the means test pension between 65 and 69 if their income is low enough, or the pension which everyone receives at 70 years of age or over. There is a distinct responsibility there which has not yet been met. I plead with the government to give consideration to it.
There are other matters, Mr. Speaker, which occur to one at this time. Perhaps the way this debate is going this is not the last stage of this throne speech debate, so I shall leave the matter at that point. It seems to me, however, that His Excellency the Governor General will be glad his term was extended for an additional period of time so that he will be able when he leaves Canada to take away with him a unique address. As the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) has pointed out, if the amendment as amended by the hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Bater) is voted for when we reach that stage, it means that the address to be delivered to the governor general on this occasion will be an address which says, "Thank you very much, sir, for your speech. It was lovely, but -." It will be an interesting point for historians to discuss in the future, as to whether the amended address was a vote of confidence or not. It will be recognized, of course, that it was just a bit of a trick, really, to get around the necessity of voting on the amendment which was put forward by my colleague the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). However, at the moment we have before us the amendment of the hon. member for Lake Centre and I am glad the house will have an opportunity of voting upon the substance of that subamendment, dealing as it does with burdensome and unnecessary taxation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The hon. member who has just spoken will forgive me, I know, if I make no effort to follow directly his line of thought. I realize quite well that anyone who delays the house in this debate at this stage in the session is most certainly not going to add to his personal popularity with this house. Nevertheless I intend to take advantage of the opportunity presented by this debate to say a few words about my recent visit to Canada's fighting forces in the Far East. I believe I should do this, because I realize that when the opportunity came my way to accompany the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) on his trip to Korea, it was not accorded to me as an individual but as a member of this house. I feel, therefore, that anything I may have learned or any

The Address-Mr. Applewhaite impressions 1 have gained should be given to this house and I would hope through this house to the country.
Let me assure hon. members that I am not going to discuss strategy in our conduct of the war. I do not feel qualified to talk on that subject. But I do feel qualified to say something about our men over there, having visited and talked with several hundred of them under actual battle conditions. I have a few notes here, but what I am going to give the house is a rambling account of our visit to these men and the impressions I gained from that visit. May I take a moment to tell hon. members that if at any time they are considering trying to find a travel companion for a visit to a battle area, they could look a long way before they would find a better one than the Minister of Fisheries. They will find that there is no terrain too difficult for him to cover; that there is no interesting spot which he will overlook; no person with whom one might converse with whom he will miss an opportunity to converse. But I should like to tell the house that he has one definite disadvantage in that he has an almost fatal attraction for enemy shellfire.
Our first contact with the forces was with the air force, who provided our transportation for the four days during which we travelled. I felt a little doubtful about the justification of some half dozen men and an airplane being tied up in order to take us around. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that we accomplished a little practical good even there. The personnel of this aircraft remained with us throughout our visit to the various units, and had an opportunity of meeting some of the navy and seeing some of the army under actual battle conditions. Two or three of these men told me that they had a much higher opinion of the surface fighter than they had before they actually saw the army and navy under battle conditions.
As the house knows, in that part of the world our air force is restricted almost entirely to the transport command. It would hardly be correct, therefore, to say that we saw the airmen under battle conditions. But I must say it was impossible to spend four days with these men, more or less dependent upon them, without coming away with the usual impression with which one always leaves the air force. The first impression is the extreme efficiency with which they carry out all their duties, and the second one is the extraordinary courtesy which they always manage to show civilians, when I am sure there are many times they could wish the civilians much farther away.
Our first actual visit was to the navy, and 1 do not know whether I should mention the

port in eastern Japan. We were fortunate enough to find two of our destroyers moored alongside each other, and I am told I might mention them by name, the Cayuga and the Sioux. We arrived there late at night and slept aboard. The following morning the ships' companies were assembled in the waists of the ships and the minister and I were able to speak to the men briefly over the public address system of both ships at the same time. This is another example of those discomforts, I suppose, which our men on active service undergo. After we had spoken over the P.A. system the men on both ships went to their mess decks and the officers went to their wardrooms; and escorted only by boatswains, we were able to visit the men in their mess decks. In other words there was not a commissioned officer around; the men could talk frankly and freely, and they did so.
Naturally the first thing one was looking for was evidence of morale. There had been so much talk about morale that I suppose it would be the first thing in the mind of any civilian who visited any of our forces in the Far East. All one can say about the morale of the navy-that part of the navy which is under actual fighting conditions at all times-is that it is absolutely tops and could not be improved upon. It is no exaggeration at all to say that the general atmosphere exuded by all the men aboard the ships was one of cheerfulness; and that was not something that was put on. They were naturally cheery fellows. When they had suggestions to make-and they had some- or personal "beefs" to bring forward, they always brought them forward with a bit of a sense of humour. They usually made a joke of even their complaints.
I asked about their mail. Their mail is coming through regularly and speedily. They told us to tell the people in Canada that there was only one trouble with the mail, and that was that they were not getting enough of it. I hope that thought may be passed on and given as wide circulation as possible. We talked about their supply of reading matter. They told me that they were well supplied with reading matter but-and this might surprise some hon. members-they said they could do with a little better diet than a constant one of "whodunits". I would not suggest to the people of Canada that they fill up our ships with Shakespeare or the Encyclopedia Britannica, but I would suggest that our men in the navy would like some of the better and more serious reading matter which is available in Canada.
Then they had a bit of a "beef"; it was not virulent, but they brought it to me several times. There had been considerable sug-

gestion in Canada at one time or another that ours was largely a dry land navy. Shorn of its picturesque naval language, what these men asked me to do when I got back to Canada was to tell the people this: We have been at sea for 29 days out of every 30 since we came out here, and on the thirtieth day when we get on shore we are back on board ship at eleven o'clock at night-for reasons which are good, considering the nature of the port they are in. Your navy out there is a navy in every sense of the word.
In order that there might be no discrimination, we visited the wardrooms as well as the mess decks and, as this house would expect me to say, we found the officers on both ships to be an outstanding group of efficient, keen young Canadians. Doubtless it was because they are of that type that the morale amongst their men was so high. So after a short visit, which was only a matter of hours in duration, one comes away with the positive conviction that, so far as Canada's navy in the Far East is concerned, they are doing a worth-while, difficult and dangerous job and are doing it well; that the men are in good health and good spirits, and that they are not suffering from the lack of things which we might be providing for them but are not.
Naturally from my point of view, and I suppose from that of anyone else, the big thrill was to visit the forces actually in Korea. In so far as Korea is concerned, this is not a travelogue. I am going to pass up any description I might be tempted to give of the country, of the damage and of the appalling poverty which is evident there amongst the civilians, except just to refer in passing to the part Canada is taking in the relief of the Korean civilians. Mr. Speaker, it is a part as to which we may feel justifiable pride. That our contribution was the first cash contribution to that service is a fact of which we may feel extremely proud.
I should like to warn this house that the time is going to come before long when a great deal more will be needed than is being done at the present time. When that time comes, Canada should not hesitate to do much more. I know the conditions there are really appallingly tragic. For immediate relief UNCACK-the United Nations civil assistance commission in Korea-which is operating under the supervision of the United States forces is doing a fine job. It is doing as much, I suppose, as any such organization could do under present conditions to meet the poverty, the cold and the distress. It is getting to nearly all but not quite all those who need its attention. That brings to mind the fact that some stories were circulated- inspired, I think, in this country at one time-
The Address-Mr. Applewhaite of the callous Canadian troops in Korea, of the brutal attitude adopted by the troops of Canada towards the civilians in Korea.
Let me tell you a little story which came to my attention while I was there. At Seoul we have a field dressing station in a farmer school building. Near that field dressing station is a Korean orphanage. To the horror of the Canadians serving in the field dressing station it was found that not long ago two small children in this orphanage died of exposure. As from that moment, to the extent that they can do so, the staff of our field dressing station are providing medical services at that orphanage, and the personnel of our Canadian army have dug up out of their own pockets $1,000 for relief and comfort for that orphanage. That shows that they are not callous or inconsiderate towards civilians. I ran into other incidents, but time will not allow me to go into them in detail. I can tell hon. members of this house quite genuinely that they can be just as proud of the character of their forces as of their fighting qualities.
In that connection I think we at home should consider carefully and tenderly the necessary monotony and discomfort experienced by those who have to serve behind the lines. While we think, quite rightly, of the heroism and sometimes the suffering of those in the actual forces, let us not forget the fact that conditions are extremely unpleasant, and they must be hard, for those who serve behind the lines in Korea without the stimulus-because it is a stimulus-of actual combat.
We visited the Canadian troops on the actual line north of the 38th parallel. Shortly after our arrival in that area we were taken by our brigade commander to an observation post on the top of a mountain almost, you might say, between the Canadian and Chinese lines, where for some two hours or more we were able to watch what was going on while the locations of the various Canadian units were pointed out to us; and while we were safe in a slit trench up to our necks we watched the effect of the artillery from both sides of the line, as well as tank fire from some of the Canadian tanks. We were there. We could hear the colonel or other observation officer transmitting back to the guns or to the tanks the actual location upon which the fire was to be directed. Then we could see, almost immediately, the fire being directed on those locations. We had good reason to see for ourselves and to appreciate the efficiency, accuracy and speed of the Canadian artillery and tank fire-and, I might mention, that of the enemy as well.

The Address

Mr. Applewhaite
We then went back to those guns, and to some of the tanks, and saw the same performance in reverse. We were back at the guns when the instructions from the observation post came in. We saw the speed and efficiency with which the orders were handled, how the gunsights were corrected by some mathematical process which remains a mystery to me. In a matter of seconds there was the report back from the observation post as to where the fire had landed.
It was shortly after that, on our first day in the battle area that, due to the fact that the Chinese also have some pretty good artillery, and that our brigade commander had things to think of other than civilians in his hair, we were sent back some five miles to an area of comparative safety. But on the following day we returned to the front lines. It was then we had the privilege of meeting the Canadian infantry. We visited two out of three of the units in the advanced position. I am told that I may mention them by name. They were the R.C.R.'s and the Van Doos. Both these regiments were visited in their extreme forward positions, just at the back of the hills facing the enemy. The forward position of the P.P.C.L.I. we were unable to go to, due to the heavy artillery fire at the time.
We spent between one and a half and two hours with each of the infantry units, meeting every officer and man on the hill with the exception of those who were actually engaged in keeping their eyes on what the Chinese were doing. We went back farther to visit an advanced dressing station; and I would like to mention this advanced dressing station, because I think it would be of interest to hon. members. It had been moved forward to its then position only five days before. The station consisted entirely of tents. It was completely manned by army personnel; there were no nurses that far forward. This dressing station was a model of spotless cleanliness and quiet efficiency. If one had to be treated for wounds or illness out in the barrens of Korea, I doubt if anything could be put up which would give a greater feeling of confidence than that advanced dressing station being maintained some few hundred yards behind the Canadian lines. That, of course, is the second point for casualties. We did not get forward to the casualty clearing post right at the front line.
Near the advanced dressing station we visited the first rear echelon, "A" echelon of the R.C.R.'s. I should like to describe that camp briefly. It is known as Peterson's paradise, and is entirely a unit affair. As fast and as

regularly as conditions allow the men of this unit are brought back from the front. This occurs roughly at ten-day intervals. They are brought to this echelon for a twelve-hour stay. There they have a hot shower bath; every stitch of clothing is taken away and replaced, not by new but by clean underwear and pressed uniforms. They have in the camp-and I do not know where they got them-a Korean barber and a Korean bootblack. A man who comes in has his bath, gets a fresh uniform, a shave and has his shoes shined and buttons polished, and for at least twelve hours out of the ten or twelve days he is a clean citizen again. There are picture shows running almost continuously. They have a certain amount of sports equipment, a softball field, and so on.
I find it difficult to imagine anything more that could be provided, within the range of enemy guns, than is being provided at "A" echelon of the R.C.R. battalion. I had the idea when I went there with a cabinet minister that, so far as possible, I would let the minister talk to the officers, the top brass, and I would try to circulate among the other ranks. I started out on that theory and to a considerable extent it was effective. The only point was that before I had been there very long I always found the minister also down among the other ranks.
The point I am trying to make is that I talked with as many as possible of the men we have out there. I did not know their names, and did not want to know them. They could talk to me absolutely without danger of being quoted. I wanted to find out what they thought, what they needed and what they wanted. I wanted to find out what their much-maligned morale really was. I found out.
Living conditions in the front line of a war can never be pleasant. Our infantrymen at the front are living on the tops of hills in Korea, in holes or tunnels from four to twelve feet deep, sand-bagged around the entrance, and deep enough-they believe and hope-to protect them from enemy mortar or shellfire other than a direct hit at the entrance. There they must live. There is nothing we can do about it, as long as we have men under wartime conditions. It is unfortunate that they must live under those conditions. Their bunkers or foxholes are reasonably warm. Fortunately, due to the terrain and the nature of the soil, there is no seepage. If the foxholes are well drained on the outside they can be dry on the inside. There is no mud on the walls or floors. They are clean, because the men who occupy them are clean and keep them clean. The water,

of -course, is not safe to drink until it has been chemically treated. Under those conditions they live; yet they maintain a cheerfulness which, quite seriously, would put to shame most members of parliament at the end of a three months' session. One would almost think-almost-that these fellows were up there on a picnic. But one does not talk to them very long before he realizes that they know just how serious a picnic it is. They do not hesitate to accept the responsibility that goes with that kind of undertaking.
I asked about their mail. It comes through from Canada in approximately nine days. They say they could do with more of it. Their statement is that while their families write to them fairly regularly, other people do not. I wonder if it would not be too much to hope that, if I were to mention this fact here, it might be broadcast further; and could one hope that those people in Canada who went to school with some of the troops in Korea, or held a job alongside some of them, would sit down once in a while and drop a note to those fellows. Do not necessarily expect them to find the time to reply. News from home is the one thing that they really crave. Another suggestion I should like to make, and I hope some organization across Canada will take it up, is with particular reference to those men who come from the little towns and communities where the local paper is published perhaps once a week. Put the home town boy on the home town newspaper subscription list. That is the sort of news our men really want.
There is only one thing that is weakening or can weaken the morale of our troops in Korea, and that is to attack them. I make that statement most seriously after having talked to a great many of them. I say to the press and the public of this country that any form of utterance belittling the morale of our men at the front is the one thing calculated to reduce that morale. Those utterances, those cartoons, those little statements have got back to the men in Korea. I know that because literally dozens of them mentioned it to me. I would be ruled- out of order if I repeated the expressions they used in mentioning it to me, but the fact is that some of these men were hurt in their feelings and thereby not at all assisted in their efficiency when they thought that we back here in Canada should doubt their morale or their ability to cope with the conditions under which they find themselves.
I checked up, because I wanted to know, the needs of the men in connection with
The Address-Mr. Applewhaite smoking, and this reminds me of cigarettes. I must correct an impression which seems to have grown up. There are no Australian cigarettes issued to our men in Korea. Australian cigarettes are issued to our men in the hospital at Kure, to which I shall refer in a minute, and at the commonwealth relief camp or base in Tokyo, both of which are administered through the commonwealth by Australia. I do not want anything I may say to deter anyone from continuing to send cigarettes to the boys in Korea, because they can use them. But I can tell you that the minister and I went to Korea with our pockets full of Canadian cigarettes. For my part I had taken them from Canada thinking they would be a treat. I found -they were a drug on the market, because in Korea our men are issued with United States cigarettes. Not only do they have the Canadian cigarettes sent to them from home, they have them when they get out because there are places at which Canadian cigarettes can be purchased.
I do not want to make this controversial, but it occurs to me that at one time there was a suggestion in Canada that we should have a commonwealth brigade. To some extent that is what we have. It is an entirely commonwealth brigade in so far as it draws its supplies entirely from Australia, including cigarettes.
While at the front I asked time after time what we in Canada were not doing that the men there thought we should be doing. It is surprising, but I could not get a positive reply. I made inquiries about mail and cigarettes, and found that both those items were coming through regularly. What I want this house to know is that I made no effort over there to whitewash this government or any branch of it. I simply wanted to find out so I could come back here and from a back bench tell the people of Canada what they were not doing and what should be done.
I have found it most difficult to find anything at all. That there are things, I do not doubt; and that they will come to our attention from time to time is a certainty, but there was no noticeable need for anything that I could find. That is why I would like the mothers and wives and relatives of our men in Korea to know, because it is the truth, that their men are in good health and good spirits. They are tough like good leather is tough, and they are proud of that toughness. They are the best fed army in -the history of the world, and to that we must give due credit to the United States because it is through them that we draw our issues.

The Address-Mr. Applewhaite Their rations include free issues of soap, smokes, razor blades, chocolate bars and other items. In the way of advice to the people of Canada, I repeat the three needs so far as the men actually on the battleline are concerned: write often and not only to the members of your family; send them the home town newspapers; criticize the government or the department if you will, but do not appear to be criticizing them.
At the conclusion of our little visit to the front we returned to Seoul and there the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) was presented with a medal ribbon-I think it came from the neck of a bottle of some description- in token of his having spent twenty-four hours under fire in Korea. I should like the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) to bear in mind that when that ribbon was presented we were assured by the senior officers of the Canadian army that it was the only truly Canadian medal ribbon so far available indicating service in Korea. I am sure the minister will see that the condition is remedied before very long.
We also visited at Kure the British commonwealth overseas forces 29th general hospital. As our time was running short, the minister and I separated, and I visited this hospital alone. I had seen what we were doing in the way of temporary quarters in an old school at Seoul, and so had great pleasure in visiting this hospital at Kure. This had been built some years ago by the Japanese as a hospital so we started with a hospital building to go into. In general terms the casualties sent to this hospital are those whom it is expected will not be able to go back to their unit within fourteen days. In other words they are going to be hospitalized for fourteen days or more. Some are not sent to Kure for special reasons; they are flown to Tokyo, Honolulu or elsewhere. There were well over one hundred Canadian patients at the Kure hospital when I was there. There were two Canadian doctors and six or eight Canadian nurses on the staff. It is a truly commonwealth hospital staffed by Australians, people from the United Kingdom and Canadians. I would say that there, as in other places in the Fair Eastern theatre, there is great room for more Canadian doctors and nurses. I talked individually to over one hundred Canadians in that hospital. Part of the time I was taken around by a Canadian doctor and part of the time by the matron, who is a Canadian. We stopped at the bed of every person who had a Canadian unit identification hung on the foot of his bed and I had a little chat with each one.
There were a few sad cases. It is perhaps no comfort to know that there must be cases of that description in any war. You cannot


have a war without having some unpleasant and serious casualties. There were a few cases in that hospital which drew me up pretty short in my tracks for a few minutes, but I am glad to say that over 90 per cent of those in the hospital at that time will completely recover with no visible major maiming. Not all were battle casualties. There was a considerable proportion of accidental casualties, and some illness, although very, very little when you consider-the conditions under which these people had been living.
Here again came up the question of morale. With the exception of the few cases to which I have referred the hospital was a cheerful, cheery place, and I am referring to the attitude of the patients. I asked them my old question: What are we not doing for you that we should do? I could get no positive reply, but people here may be interested in knowing the two questions asked me most often by Canadian patients in that hospital. The first was: Who is the leading contender for the Grey cup, and the second was: What is the weather like back home? These are the things about which these men are thinking. Their mail is coming through well and they are well supplied with cigarettes and reading matter.
I asked one fellow: "How are you making out"? He said, "All right. Why the so-and-so wouldn't we be? We have Canadian nurses." I should like other Canadian nurses to remember that, because I think we could use more of them. I want to tell you of one case, a lad with a broken elbow and other arm injuries caused by shrapnel. He was a young fellow from Montreal. He asked me what the weather was like in Montreal when I left Canada. I told him as best I knew and made some inane remark such as: "I suppose you are hoping soon to see it for yourself". He said: "Oh, no. I was only up on the hill for thirty-six hours when I stopped this one. I do not want to go home yet. We have a job to do." And there are people in Canada who have dared to talk about the low morale of the Canadian forces!
The hospital draws its supplies through the Australians, and as many of us know the Australians lean heavily to mutton. I was a little worried in chatting to one fellow who was flat on his back. He was giving me a long line of criticism about the endless diet of mutton. I thought he really had a genuine complaint until I suddenly discovered he had finally got a rise out of the man in the next bed, who was an Australian. That was typical of the hospital. The patients would kid back and forth among themselves. If they had a serious complaint they turned it into a joke.

You learn one or two lessons, or think you do, from a trip of that sort. Hon. members may recall that when this debate first started we had an eloquent speech by the hon. member for Beauharnois (Mr. Cauchon) in which he referred to national unity. I should like to tell the hon. member that if he wants to see national unity he should go to the battlefields of Korea and see the Royal Canadian Regiment, the Princess Patricia's and the Van Doos side by side. He should see them side by side in hospital beds at Kure. I can assure him that none of them care a bit whether a man first learned from his mother to speak French, English with a Scotch brogue, or Ukrainian and then came to Canada and learned one of the other languages. There you have national unity and national respect. I did not hear anybody from the Van Doos complaining because some colonel spoke English. I did not hear anybody from the R.C.R.'s or the P.P.C.L.I.'s complaining because other fellows, who were doing their share of the job, learned to speak French before they spoke English. There are no language difficulties over there. When you get down to the realities of life people have no time to worry about those factors which unfortunately at times would appear-and it is only an appearance-to disrupt our national unity.
One comes back from Korea very proud of the Canadian forces. One would not be human if after spending a few days there, seeing these men in action and hearing the Americans, Australians and others talk about them, one was not also very proud of being a Canadian. You cannot go out there, meet these fellows and see them on the line and in the hospitals without feeling pretty humble in the face of what they are and what they are doing, officers and men alike, army, navy and air force. As strongly as I know how I should like to make a suggestion to the members of this house, the press and the public of this country. First let me make it clear that so far as I am concerned there is no reason why anyone should hesitate to make constructive criticism whenever it is due. But-and I say this only because it was mentioned to me so often over there-give some thought to the effect what you are going to say or write will have on the men who are actually doing the fighting and living in the mud.
We in this house regard ourselves as public servants. We know that we and other public servants are fit subjects for criticism and public discussion. It might be said that the Canadian army and navy are also public
The Address-Mr. H. O. White services and therefore they should be criticized and discussed. I do not enjoy it when somebody undertakes to take me to pieces or explain where I have shortcomings as a member of parliament, but how much more hurtful it is for our soldiers and sailors to be taken to pieces to find out what is making them fall short of what they should be as soldiers and sailors when they are not falling short of what they should be at all. If you and I are criticized, Mr. Speaker, we have our right of reply here in the house. The men over there have no right of reply. They can make only one reply. If their morale is attacked it is a suggestion that they are not the type of soldiers they should be, and the only reply they can make is by a demonstration of the way they meet the enemy and put up with the conditions they have to face. I think they have made the reply and made it very effectively. I left Korea with one very strong impression, and that was that the best morale in Canada is in Korea.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I make no apologies for entering the debate at this late stage of the session. My remarks are based on the unemployment situation in the city of London and the surrounding district. On November 19 I addressed the following question to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg):
I should like to ask the Minister of Labour what steps, if any, have been or are being taken to alleviate the serious mounting unemployment in London, Ontario.
At that time the Minister of Labour replied as follows:
I do not think the seriousness of the unemployment situation is as great as my hon. friend implies in his question, but X can assure him that we are keeping in close touch wtih the situation.
This was on November 19, and ever since that day the unemployment situation has become more acute. I hold in my hand the figures as of December 1, issued by the national employment service in London, Ontario. Comparing them with the same date a year ago we see that on December 1, 1950, some 1,381 were unemployed. Today there are 2,857. This says nothing whatever about at least 800, and probably more, that are on a very short work week. It says nothing whatever about those who have not registered with the national employment service as being out of work. I want to point out to the house the industries that are most seriously affected, and I give them in the order in which they were given to me as those most seriously affected. The first is General Steel Wares, Adelaide street plant; second, General Steel Wares, York street plant; third, Kel-vinator of Canada; fourth, General Motors diesel; fifth, Eaton Automotive Products

The Address-Mr. H. O. White Limited; and sixth, Empire Brass Manufacturing Company. What I want to point out is the fact that all these companies are engaged in the processing of metals; in other words, they are firms that could be and should be producing the sinews of war.
In trying to arrive at the root causes of the situation two things of course come uppermost. One is the credit curtailment. We have inflation caused by this government; then where they turn around and try to fight it the men who are being injured the most are those in the industries that we need to keep operating to produce the munitions of war. The second cause is the shortage of steel. That of course goes back a long way. Steel is vital in our industrial life. Since I have mentioned that, I may say that I hold in my hand sessional paper 161, issued in the name of the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough). It shows the imports of steel from the United States to Canada, and also the production in tons in Canada. Without going into detail about it may I say it shows that the imports from the United States have been going up consistently every month but one. Ten months of 1951 are shown in this return. It also shows that while there has been a slight increase in the production of steel in Canada, that increase is not very great. In fact it is hardly noticeable in our over-all production of steel.
I want to point out also that in the defence production report, issued for the period October 16 to October 31, 1951, only two defence orders went to the city of London in western Ontario, and those two together amounted to only $79,374. During that two-week period some $35 million worth of contracts were let in Canada. That does not of course include the $630,000 contract for the construction of a barrack block in the city of London. But I am pointing out that so far as steel and metals are concerned very few, if any, contracts came to the city of London. In fact one contract for $62,585 went to a paper box company, and the other for communication equipment amounted to $16,789. We have in the city of London a good many firms working in steel, yet we have idle men at a time when we are facing a relentless enemy and the sinews of war are steel. I would say that it is nothing short of criminal negligence to have idle men at a time like this when we are buying time, Mr. Speaker, in Europe and in Asia so the western world can prepare to meet the enemy, and also to prepare our defences.
Some will say the reason the companies in London are not working at full time, or that there is unemployment there, is the allotment of steel to essential industry, those industries that are working on war orders. Such is not


the case, Mr. Speaker, because I know of one firm there which has 50 per cent of its men laid off. They are working on war orders, and the men have been laid off because they are not getting the steel.
Another angle that is pretty provoking is the fact that if a steel concern in Canada is affiliated with a United States firm they are able to secure prefabricated steel from the United States, while the purely Canadian firms are left holding the bag and their men are idle. This is a very serious situation. We are again on the short end of a bad deal as far as arrangements with the United States are concerned.
I want to point out to the house the export of vital war materials that we produce in Canada in abundance. I am just going to mention two of them, namely aluminum and copper. We find that in 1946 we exported aluminum to the value of $56 million, in 1950 to the tune of $106 million and in the first ten months of 1951 to the tune of $108 million. In 1946 we exported $37 million worth of copper; in 1950, $87 million worth, and in the first ten months of 1951, $66 million worth. The United States are receiving these-vital war metals, but when it comes to steeL coming back into Canada we are being given a rather raw deal. I bring this matter to the attention of the house to point out that in London we have these idle men, and the situation is worse than the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) suggested in his reply .to me. I had the opportunity to attend a meeting in London last Thursday when industry, labour and welfare organizations, including Catholic charities, all met and this position was explained to us. The people in charge of the charities said that at the present rate of welfare being dispersed by these organizations in the city of London their funds would be exhausted long before the end of the fiscal year.
There is another angle to it that does not appear on the surface. Take a plant that is fabricating steel. Labour in the plant see that the supply of steel is running short, so they slow down in their work. That is what you and I would do if we were in the same position. They try to spin the work out as long as they can, and the net result is that our defence dollar is only buying about 25 cents worth of material. There are three things that could happen: unemployment, the high cost of the end product, or financial ruin for the firm. This is the situation many of these people are facing.
Rumours were abroad that it was part of government policy to have a certain amount

of unemployment in order to obtain recruits for the army. I hope that is not true, but it indicates how seriously the people are viewing the situation. They are calling it a lefthanded recruiting drive.
Black and grey markets exist. I was made aware of the fact that quotations on certain types of steel were in this ratio: the Canadian price for a certain product is 31 and the United States price is 46. This is an indication of what the cost of some of these goods would be when finished. I just want to draw the situation so far as steel is concerned to the attention of the house. It was brought to the attention of the house by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), who quoted the following few sentences from Time magazine:
By 1952's end. Jones and Laughlin will have spent $390 million in six years, boosted its capacity by 32 per cent. By the same time, Bethlehem-big steel's chief rival-will have spent $700 million, boosted its capacity 36 per cent since 1946. Inland is spending $145 million, Republic $250 million, . . .
This gives an indication of the increase planned for steel production across the border. Then, in Time magazine of December 10, 1951, there is an article entitled "Steel Surgery". It reads in part as follows:
After Washington fixed Canada's allocation of U.S. steel for the first quarter of 1952 at 415,050 tons, Ottawa gulped in dismay; it had asked for a rock bottom minimum of 527,809 tons. The news meant an unexpected 9 per cent slice in the overall supply. The government had long ago clamped down on non-essential steel construction. Last week it began to cut into the muscle of other civilian uses almost as ruthlessly as it did during world war II.
I would suggest that another item that is adding to cost is the fact that tenders for war orders require a deposit of 10 per cent. One department of the government under the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) cashes these cheques and apparently uses the funds as working capital, while the other department holds the cheques as a deposit. These two departments are under the one minister. I suggest that where the cheques are cashed the production cost of that firm is higher than in the case where the cheque is not cashed. The firm whose cheque is cashed has to pay a higher rate of interest than does the one whose cheque is not cashed. I have brought this serious situation to the attention of the house, and I hope the minister will take more action than he did when I first brought the matter to his attention.

Can my hon.
friend remember when the debate began?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Some time in the month before last. I listened with pleasure to what the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) said about Lord Alexander, the governor general, who is a great governor and a great man. It was my privilege to suggest some time ago that his term should be extended, and this was finally done. I am not going to suggest the name of anyone to replace His Excellency when his term is ended. That is a matter to be dealt with by the government and His Majesty the King. I have nothing to say as to whether we should have a Canadian citizen or a British subject to represent His Majesty the King in this country. I leave that matter to the government. The only warning I give to the government is this. If the suggestion made by some papers is adopted, namely that Mr. Arthur Meighen be appointed governor general, it would perhaps lead to a movement for annexation to the United States. But it is quite improbable that such a suggestion would be adopted.
I was delighted to pay my respects to Her Royal Highness The Princess Elizabeth when she came to my constituency. I had the privilege of paying to her the same compliment that I paid to her mother, Her Majesty the Queen, when she came to visit this country a few years ago, namely that she had conquered all hearts. The Canadian National Railways did things well in my constituency. The station at Riviere du Loup was painted. The stations at Cacouna, at St. Eloi, and St. Arsene were also painted. As the station at Isle Verte was new, it was the big tank that was painted by the railway. They wanted to prepare the reception quite properly.
Mr. Speaker, we hear so many criticisms about everything that tonight it is my intention to thank the government and the whole house for what has been done for my constituency during these last few years, especially with regard to the fire that destroyed the village of Cabano and also the one that, a few days afterwards, destroyed Rimouski. There are

The Address-Mr. Pouliot many people whom I must thank on behalf of those who have rebuilt that village quite well. At first it was the army that gave great assistance to the people. Station CJFP at Riviere du Loup was there, kept the people informed, and secured some help. After the fire the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Langlois) and I interviewed the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and Mr. Mansur of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to ask them what could be done. My good friend Mr. Wilbur Arkison, a prominent journalist of Montreal, published a front-pgge interview in the Montreal Standard three days after the fire. All the newspapers gave their support to the victims of the fire. His Worship the Mayor of Montreal, who is also the member for Papineau, organized a great meeting at the Forum to come to the assistance of victims of the fires at Rimouski and Cabano, and the net profit was between $6,000 and $7,000. My colleagues of the house were kind enough to direct people who were sending food and clothing to both places. A genial maritimer by the name of Alistair Fraser who is a dear friend of mine and who is a prominent railway man succeeded in giving Cabano and the Temiseouata Railway milling in transit rates, which were extremely helpful to the lumbermen of that part of the county. I remember the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) was kind enough to pay a visit to Cabano, and succeeded in comforting the people. He wanted to see the extent of the damage, and he spoke to them in encouraging terms. At that meeting there were two local members of my com-te who were there to pay homage to the Prime Minister of Canada. They were two members of the provincial legislation.
A report was made by the commissioners early in May. There was an understanding between the federal and provincial governments with regard to the amount that was to be provided by Ottawa and the province for purposes of relief. I express my thanks to the Prime Minister of Canada as well as to Mr. Duplessis for what has been done in that respect.
Also I received word from Mr. St. John Chadwick, first consul at the office of the High Commissioner for Great Britain, who brought gifts from the United Kingdom to the people of Cabano. They were most generous gifts including some chinaware, some clothes, some shoes; all sorts of things. There were very precious gifts of silverware sent by the nobility of England to the people of Cabano and Rimouski.
I was there with Mr. John Lewis, deputy secretary of state for the commonwealth, who

came to Cabano with Mr. Chadwick. I attended the distribution of gifts from Great Britain to the people of my constituency. I offer special thanks to my colleagues of the House of Commons, because the whip, the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Tremblay) gave me a cheque for $505 contributed for Cabano by members of parliament. Also our lamented friend, the Hon. Humphrey Mitchell, told me that he had sent directly to the mayor of Cabano his personal cheque for $50. Then Hon. Liaqua-t Ali Khan, deceased premier of Pakistan, when he came to Ottawa subscribed $1,000 for the relief of the victims of the fires at Rimouski and Cabano. This was most generous of him.
I must not only thank the Prime Minister of Canada and the premier of Quebec, but I must congratulate them upon the appointment of the commissioners, Brigadier Antonin Theriault of Quebec city and Mr. Edouard Laurent of Quebec. Brigadier Theriault was the representative of the Ottawa government and Mr. Laurent represented the government of Quebec. Then they had as a third commissioner His Worship Emilien Morin of Cabano, who did splendid work to assist his fellow citizens.
There are only one or two points in this connection I would like to mention. The first is that in those two fires the compagnie de pouvoir du Bas Saint-Laurent charged $26,522, and the corporation de telephone de Quebec charged $53,439 for damages suffered by them at Rimouski. These amounts were paid to these companies. Perhaps they got more, I do not know. On the other hand, I must tell the house that the compagnie de telephone de Kamouraska, whose president is Mr. F. C. Whitaker of Montreal, suffered damages to the extent of more than $4,000, by reason of the Cabano fire, but -they were generous enough to cancel their claim. It was their contribution on behalf of those who had suffered in the fire. Hon. members may judge from this the difference of approach in a matter of this kind. The compagnie de telephone de Kamouraska was public-spirited and generous, while the other two companies were very greedy. This is not new.
And, sir, I want to say something about the Canadian National Railways. I will tell you that all my life, especially since the beginning of my public career as a member of parliament, I have been a strong advocate of the Canadian National Railways, that big organization -that goes from coast to coast. I happen to live at a divisional point in the Intercolonial section of the national railway company. At the beginning Riviere du Loup was the eastern terminal of the Grand Trunk

Railway, before the construction of the Intercolonial Railway. If railway employees can claim seniority rights, then the shops must have the same right. The shops at Riviere du Loup must have seniority over all other shops of the Canadian National Railways. This is ignored. There are big shops at Moncton, at Point St. Charles, as well as at Stratford, Ontario, and at Transcona, which is not far from Winnipeg. But the shops at Riviere du Loup existed long before these others were built. No one spoke about them at that time.
We live in strange times, times of centralization. Some people who are called men of vision see only one thing, a huge thing, a tower of Babel; the bigger it is, the better it is. Well, that is absurd. Why do we, have a housing problem? Why did we have such a problem, especially after the war? It was more acute then than it is now, because some progress has been made, although matters have not yet been completely adjusted. It is precisely because of the ex'odus of people from the country to the city, due to that centralization of industry. I remember some years ago' I told a story of the Noiseless Land Company or La Com-pagnie des Terrains sans Bruit Ltee., at Quebec city. There were two gentlemen, two politicians rather, Philippe Pelletier and Mr. Perodeau. They formed a partnership to buy some swamp land near Quebec city at a very low price. Laurier was in power and they offered this land to the Laurier government. Laurier said, "No, I will never buy it." Then Pelletier became postmaster general in the Borden government, and as he was allpowerful the Borden government bought the Noiseless Land Company's property from Pelletier, Perodeau and company at a high figure.
After the swamp had been bought it had to be used because they were afraid of a scandal. So they built shops on that soft soil and after the shops were built they needed men and machinery. They took the men and machinery from Riviere du Loup for the new shops built on the Noiseless Land property. It was like the deportation of the Acadians. It was a great blow to my city. The shops continued to exist and some time afterward Sir Henry Thornton, president of the Canadian National Railways, decided to reduce the personnel of the Riviere du Loup shops to a minimum. I tried to argue with him but it served no purpose. But Hon. Charles Dunning, supported by the late Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, saw to it that there was no reduction. The men who had been sent away came back to work in the shops.
The Address-Mr. Pouliot
That was a great advantage, not because of politics but because the Riviere du Loup shops were an asset to the community. Afterwards the St. Malo shops were closed for railway business and this work was transferred to the Department of National Defence. At the outset of the war Moncton tried to place its clutching hands on the fine machinery that was there, but Mr. Hungerford saw to it that that should not happen and the machinery that was billed to Moncton was rebilled to Riviere du Loup. The men who had been forced to leave their homes had an opportunity to come back to Riviere du Loup to continue their work for the railroads. They do most excellent work.
That was the third time we suffered from centralization. Quebec does not need a railway shop any more than a dog needs two tails. Why? The St. Malo shops were built simply to cover a scandal under a Tory government.

No scandal. I will fight to
the death to maintain the rights of my constituents who continue to do splendid work at Riviere du Loup for the Canadian National Railways. I am not impressed by the advocates of centralization who are bringing about the downfall of the railway. We are asking for two shifts, a day shift and a night shift. If we have the number of men that we need at Riviere du Loup we will be able to compete with any shops anywhere on the Canadian National Railways. We are between the Point St. Charles and Moncton shops, between New Brunswick and Montreal. I am a friend of the maritimes and I am ready to co-operate with them provided they do not try to cut our throats.

No. I hope my hon. friend will be good enough to stop at Riviere du Loup the next time he passes that way and I will bring him to the shops where he can meet the men who witnessed these incidents. They are in a better position than I to give specific details. I have never said anything in the house that I did not believe was accurate.
Not only do we want to have two shifts at Riviere du Loup instead of one; it is also important that the work started last summer by the Canadian National Railways to repair the right of way of the Temiscouata railway be continued next year. Why should that be done? There is only one line on the Intercolonial between Montreal and Levis and Halifax, which line runs through Moncton. It is essential that there be a double line from Riviere du Loup onward and the Temiscouata railroad should be repaired so it can serve to its utmost capacity. A highway, which is part of highway No. 2 between Toronto and Halifax, has been completed and will be paved next year. It is one of the finest highways in Canada. The scenery is just as grand at that north of Montreal with mountains and large lakes, such as lake Temiscouata. But this is lumbering country. Thanks to what has been done by Mr. Alistair Fraser, a former vice-president of the Canadian National-and I give credit to the management for this-the milling in transit rate given to lumber producers near the Temiscouata line and in the back country would do marvels if they were supplied with enough cars. I could mention some prominent lumbermen in my part of the country. One of them is well known throughout the country because he is a former president of the Canadian Lumbermen's Association. I refer to Mr. Raoul Guerette of Estcourt who asked the railway last winter for 5,000 cars to ship lumber from Whitworth to other points. Whitworth is on the Temiscouata line. He could not get all the cars. At the meetings of the railways and shipping committee last session I questioned Mr. Dingle about it. I knew very well it was true because I was the one who sent a wire to the management on behalf of Mr. Guerette to have the 5,000 cars sent there.
The Temiscouata railway is serving a purpose. We hear about the claims for improvement that come from various parts of the country. Members ask many things from the government. I make my claim, and I am


sincere, honest and earnest about it. I am sure the government will support my request because it is in the public interest. I want the completion of the repairing of the track of the Temiscouata railway so that it can be used for heavy traffic. There is supposed to be an extension of the Matane railway to Gaspe. I have no objections to it, but if there is enough money to continue the Matane branch to Gaspe there must be enough to finish the Temiscouata line so it will give the railway the profit it is entitled to get from it. I will have other occasions to mention this matter, but I rely on the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), the government and the whole house to give us what we are entitled to have.
There are maritime rights. There are also Temiscouata rights and the rights of every other constituency in this country. I am only too proud to be the advocate of the rights of Temiscouata and to defend my constituents. Once I attended the blessing of the cornerstone of a hospital, and the bishop was there. I told him: Sir, you are the spiritual father of these nice people; I am their temporal father. You look after their interests in heaven and I look after their interests in this world. I am sure I shall have the support of the government and the house in the redressing of all wrongs and seeing to it that Temiscouata is not treated as a country cousin.
The last thing I have to say is about the pensions of railway employees. I discussed the matter in the railways and shipping committee last year. The hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Dube) made some very good speeches about it. I refer to the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island Railway employees provident fund. There are 4,850 contributors and 3,300 pensioners. Monthly payments are $300,000. There are 2,200 who receive more than $90, 650 who receive from $50 to $90 and 450 who receive from $30 to $50. It is not much when we think of it. That is another matter that I brought to the attention of the management, and it is a shame.
Before the Temiscouata railway was purchased by the government it was operating in great difficulties. There are some men who after working for the Temiscouata railway for half a century receive much less than $30 a month as a pension. They receive $5. The management of the Canadian National say they have no responsibility. How can that be? The monthly cheques of $5 are signed by the Canadian National Railways. It is a shame, and any other organization would

increase these pensions. There are other things that I might say. I do not envy anyone what he has got for his constituency. The government looked after Temiscouata. Les electeurs de mon comte have received due consideration in the applications they have made, and they are among those in the country who every time thank not only the government but the Prime Minister and the other ministers concerned for what they do for them. It is a very fine tradition and they never fail.
But, sir, I am sure after the expose of the facts that I have related to the house tonight they will again have occasion to thank the government and also the Canadian National Railways. We are not opposed to the railways. We do not want them to do anything that is not in the public interest, but we want them to serve every part of the country as well as possible. My friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) has just taken his seat. He is doing something for Temiscouata. He built a fine wharf at Riviere du Loup. He has just bought a nice tract of land for a public building which is required for the post office, the unemployment insurance commission, the customs, the mounted police and other departments. With the support of my hon. colleagues, I am sure a fine building will be erected on that land in the very near future.
I also want an airport at Riviere du Loup for civilian use and for purposes of military defence. It is time to have it. All the plans are ready, and I am sure it will come in due course. I am just about through. I thank the house for their kind attention and, moreover, the inspiration my colleagues have given me while I have been speaking. I cannot pay a better compliment to my colleagues than to say that tonight I felt just as much at home as if I had been in my own constituency.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take the opportunity tonight to draw your attention to the fact that persecution of Canadian nationals by the Chinese communists is increasing at an alarming rate. One week ago today it was drawn to the attention of the Prime Minister that two Canadian nuns had been sentenced to five years imprisonment and three other Canadian nuns had been ordered deported on the fantastic charge that they had murdered children under their care.
It is obvious from the evidence which was presented, at what passes for a trial in communist countries, that these children were past all hope of recovery when they were delivered to the orphanage, and that it was
The Address-Mr. Hees only the Christianity of those nuns which caused them to admit those children and do what they could for them whilst life still remained.
The evidence that these five nuns are completely innocent is overwhelming, and does not need to be elaborated at this time. What the Chinese communists violently objected to was the fact that these nuns were teaching and demonstrating Christianity.
Following this outrage, we read in this morning's paper that two nuns and a priest were forced to exhume children's bodies in the area near Canton. They were forced to work twelve hours a day for twelve days, without rest and with very little food, and the citizens in the vicinity were encouraged to taunt them while they were at their task.
Again in this morning's paper we read that a Canadian priest, Right Rev. Gustave Prevost, was arrested two months ago by the Chinese communists and is now reported as having confessed to having been a spy. Those who are familiar with communist methods will realize that whatever false confession he is claimed to have given could only have been forced from him by privation and torture.
I believe that the time has come for the government to tell the Canadian people what steps it plans to take to protect Canadian citizens against the kind of outrages I have just described.
