After listening to the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) I am sure that the few words I have to say tonight will be more or less in order. He spoke about the various things that were going on in China, and that brings me to say that here in the house we were lobbied today by a group of people who were representing the peace congress. This afternoon I had a group of them in my room for about an hour, and after letting each one say what he had to say I had my turn in questioning them. To be truthful, I believe that some of these people are sincere in their efforts to obtain peace. When I questioned some of them I asked point-blank whether there were any communists in their organization, and I was informed that there were.
They wanted to know what members of parliament were doing to bring peace throughout the world. I told them that Canada, representing approximately 15 million people, could not bring about peace by itself, but that I had every confidence in the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), through whom Canada speaks, and in our Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), and I was sure that we were doing everything we could to preserve peace.

The Address-Mr. Sinnott
They asked me questions; they asked whether I did not think it would be far better if instead of spending what we are spending now on arms we spent it on peaceful purposes. I think we tall agree on that, but I asked them how it was that our enemy, or what we think is our enemy at the present time, was building up armed forces of over 2,800,000 men at the present time, and that we did not have the right to go in there to see at what rate they were building up those arms and other weapons of war. I also told them that from my experience in many disputes in our own councils at home I thought it could be done better by negotiation than with guns.

During the sixteen years of my membership in this house I have never yet undertaken to tell the members of the house about my particular constituency. I believe it would be well for me in a short time tonight to depart from that custom which I have established and give the members some idea of the kind of disaster whioh has overtaken many areas in Alberta.
Normally my constituency is one of the most prosperous in the dominion, judged from the amount of income tax my constituents pay, and altogether it is rather remarkable for the amount of well-being which prevails there. Here are some of the things that have happened this year:	In the first
place, we had rain in the spring which delayed seeding a month. Everybody who knows anything about agriculture understands how serious that is. We could have recovered from that quite readily, I believe, if we had had a chance, but we did not have a chance.


It kept on raining too often all summer long, thereby delaying maturity. Although the crop, with abundant rainfall and the kind of weather we generally have there in respect of sunlight and so on, was excellent, yet it was not harvested. Snow laid very much of it down before it could be cut. Much of the grain that was not laid down by snow had been swathed, and consequently was subject to the deteriorating influence of too much moisture during rather warm weather while in contact with the soil. In most cases what was harvested was too damp to be stored with safety. The result was that, in a large measure, people lost their grain crop.
Ordinarily, in my constituency, a great deal of hay is produced. We had a very fine crop because of the rain, but almost as though there had been a committee of fiends appointed to supervise what went on during the summer, we had rain just often enough to catch every cutting of hay in the windrow and destroy it. Some of you have had that experience; that condition followed us right through the season. The result was that most of the hay was spoiled in the windrow or in the bundle. A number of people are now beginning to bind the hay in bundles for protection, but the bundles were spoiled; they turned just as black as a stove. What little hay was harvested and stacked in good condition was utterly destroyed by a heavy rain in September, which soaked through from the top of the stack to the ground. In a district that does a great deal of livestock raising, hon. members can realize how tragic that experience was.
There are three'sugar beet factories in my constituency. Normally the beet crop is the surest crop the people have, and this is especially true of the irrigated areas. Beet germination was delayed because of the wet weather I spoke about, and in some places there was so much dampness that the young beets were killed when they first came up. The beets did not progress as they should have, and when harvesting time arrived the weather was so wet it was exceedingly difficult to harvest the beets. Many of the growers have beet harvesting machines which were unable to function because of the moisture in the soil. Where they did function there was great expense in harvesting the beets. Finally, a great number of beets were frozen in the ground. The loss in the beet industry has been severe.
My constituency is one of the best in Canada for producing cattle. There are many ranchers, and they would have experienced a successful season because of the fine pasture during the summer except for the fact that the hay crop was destroyed. Then it was impossible to harvest the grain crop

and the ranchers were unable to get access to the straw upon which many of them depend for carrying their animals through. The result has been that many of the stockmen have been forced to get rid of their stock just in the year they were depending upon stock because of the losses in other crops upon which they relied. Those cattlemen who usually pasture their stock in the fields after the grain is harvested were unable to do so this year because much of the grain lay either uncut or in the swath. If they turned their stock into the field they would founder by eating too much of the grain.
In my area there is a good deal of sheep feeding and sheep raising. Ordinarily the feeders turn their sheep into the fields to pasture on the beet tops which are left in the fields after the beets are harvested. Those who have sheep are in serious difficulties because of the poor beet harvest, and in some cases are being forced to dispose of their flocks.
One of the major industries is the feeding of beef cattle and sheep during the winter. The beet pulp which comes from the manufacture of sugar from beets is probably the finest feed for cattle that is known to man. The pulp alone is not so very good for the cattle, and it is necessary to have with it hay or straw. This year the hay and straw are lacking or have to be brought great distances at tremendous cost. The result will be that this major industry will be largely a failure this year, except in a very few cases.
I believe this picture, a rather gloomy one, which I have drawn of my constituency gives some idea of the suffering of the people in Alberta. Something ought to be done. I do not know what the government has in mind, but it appears to me to be almost an emergency. It should be called at least a provincial emergency, but it is beyond the financial competence of the province to deal with it. It seems to me it becomes almost a national emergency, especially when we recall that Saskatchewan is afflicted almost as seriously as Alberta.
May we go back to the discussions of last spring and recall that the farmers were able to establish that, as a result of the sale of wheat under the British-Canadian wheat agreement, they had lost money. This was established largely through such spokesmen as the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair), the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) and others. Considering all the factors which entered into the situation, it was proved that the farmers lost hundreds of millions of dollars.
It will be recalled that the government listened to their appeals to the extent of
The Address-Mr. Blackmore contributing $65 million towards reimbursing the farmers for those losses. It will be recalled that there was talk of $48 million being paid as compensation for another disability which the farmers suffered. Members from those areas continued to discuss the $48 million question until I was ruled out of order on April 6 for undertaking to discuss it. An amendment had been moved by the C.C.F. calling for payment of the $48 million, and when the vote was taken on that amendment further discussion of the $48 million was ruled out. That might have been a contribution to the well-being of the farmers and it might not, depending on how one looked at it.
I wonder if it would not be wise for us to consider the advisability of going back and taking another look at that $48 million proposition., to see whether or not it would be a good thing for this government now to pay that amount to western farmers. It would give those who are suffering at least some money with which to buy the children something for Christmas, and some money with which to help the merchants who are almost in despair in my constituency because they have advanced credit to the farmers, hoping for a crop, and now find themselves in the grip of the wholesalers and utterly lost to know where to turn in order to be able to carry on until spring. In that respect $48 million would help all the way around.
If I may be pardoned for reading from my remarks last spring, I should like to refer to page 1300 of Hansard of the first session of 1951. On March 15 I closed my speech with these words:
As I have previously argued, the wheat producers ought to receive compensation to the extent of at least 25 cents per bushel. The people of Canada through the dominion government are in duty bound to pay that 25 cents. Britain, let me repeat, has not the least scintilla of a moral obligation in any shape or form in connection with reimbursing Canadian farmers for the losses they have sustained by reason of the British-Canadian wheat agreement.
I had argued that matter so fully, I think, that there could be no answer to the argument I had adduced showing that the British had no obligation, contractual or moral, in any way.
Then, if I may, I should like to turn to page 1716 of Hansard of April 6, and read my closing remarks on that occasion:
As I say, I am closing my remarks tonight, but this is not the last I am going to say in advocacy of the proposition that the dominion government at an early date contribute $48 million more to the pool fund for the farmers of western Canada.
Tonight I am making good that promise. Inasmuch as all this is more than six months old, it might be wise for us to give some attention to the story behind the $48 million so that people who are not familiar with

The Address-Mr. Blackmore the situation will be able to understand what it is all about. What is the story behind this $48 million request?
Between March 1, 1945 and February 17, 1947, some 160 million bushels of wheat were consumed by Canadians. The wheat board sold this wheat to Canadian millers at 77-3/8 cents per bushel. The Canadian government paid the wheat board an additional 47-5/8 cents per bushel, making a total of $1.25 per bushel to go into the fund from which the farmers were to be paid, all that they were to get by reason of the sale of wheat to Britain during the four-year period. If that wheat had been sold to Britain the farmers would have received $1.55 per bushel. If sold to any other nation but Canada the farmers would have received more than. $1.55 a bushel, for then their wheat would have become class II wheat which in many oases sold at a much higher figure than $1.55. The farmers therefore lost at least 30 cents on every one of those 160 million bushels of wheat which the Canadian people consumed. In other words they lost .160 million times 30 cents, or $48 million.
As it worked out, this $48 million was a definite subsidy paid by the farmers to bring down the price of bread, or at least the price of the wheat that entered into the bread which Canadians ate during the period I have indicated.
The farmers not only paid this $48 million as a direct consumers' subsidy to bring down the price of bread; they also paid, through their taxes, a share of the 47-5/8 cents a bushel which the Canadian government paid the wheat board to help make up the $1.25. Surely the farmers are entitled to that $48 million! I do not think any line of reasoning can be advanced or any evidence can possibly be adduced by anyone which can show that the conclusion I have drawn is unsound.
When the government last spring paid the $65 million to the farmers, many hon. members argued that it ought not to have been paid. Hon. members of the house can recall men who rose in their places and sincerely argued in that way. Most of those men felt that the dominion had no obligation to pay this money.
What sort of reasoning influenced hon. members in opposing assistance to the farmers then? There were several considerations. By members of the cabinet and others it was argued that the British-Canadian wheat agreement was an experiment in price and market stabilization. It was therefore argued that what the farmers lost was a sort of premium such as men would pay on an insurance policy to guarantee that they would have markets and reasonably stable

prices. I was not impressed with the argument, but a good many hon. members were.
Again it was argued that if the 600 million bushels of wheat that Canada sold to Britain during the four years had been thrown on the markets of the world, the price of class II wheat would have been forced down and consequently it would have been impossible to show that the farmers had lost money by selling to Britain at $1.55. The general idea seemed to be that it would be quite impossible to tell how far the price would have been forced down, and that it might possibly have been forced down even below $1.55. This thought seemed to be in men's minds.
Then others argued that if Canada had not sold the 600 million bushels to Britain she probably could not have sold that wheat at all, but would have found her wheat crowded out of the world markets by competitors.
I think probably a bit of evidence that people would accept as worth considering would be in order at the present time. I should like to read a statement from the April 11, 1951 Searle Grain Company's letter. Before I start to read this, may I say that I recall how greatly exercised some hon. members became last year because I referred to the Searle Grain Company's letter. I argued-and I think soundly-that I had never known the Searle Grain Company to make any errors in figures. They make errors in their conclusions and their reasoning, I grant you that; but their figures are sound. This quotation I am about to give contains figures which can be expressed in their words quite as effectively as they can be expressed in mine, and they will carry with them the authority of the Searle Grain Company. I quote from the letter as follows:
If the 600 million (150 million a year for each of four years) had been offered on the open market then, of course, Britain would not have purchased this wheat under contract, but she would have had to buy from somewhere the same quantity to feed her people for her people were seriously short of food. Britain, therefore, would have had to come to the open market with demands at the rate of 150 million a year, or 600 million in four years. This extra 600 million of demand would have exactly balanced the 600 million of extra supply, so price would not have been affected. Experienced grain men are convinced that the open market price for all our wheat over the four years would most probably have been even higher than the class II rates.
That is their conclusion. I am not saying anything about that.
Could all our wheat have been sold had it not been for the agreement? Most certainly it could have been. During these four years the United States sold on world markets 1,932,000,000 bushels; Argentina sold 373,000,000 bushels; Australia 433,000,000 bushels and Canadian class II wheat 196,000,000 bushels, or a total of 2,934,000,000 bushels and all was

sold at class II or better than class II price. France, India, Turkey and Russia also sold unrevealed additional amounts, again at high prices.
For the first three years the world was badly short of food, The world was even buying Canadian rye at $4.83 a bushel-worth usually 20 per cent less than wheat-and registered seed wheat for making into flour at $6 a bushel. Britain herself was buying wheat from the U.S.A., Australia, Argentina, Turkey and some say from Russia and at prices higher than class II prices.
What reason, then, have we to suppose that Britain or any other buying country would have paid less for Canadian wheat than they did for other wheats lower in quality, and while the world demand considerably exceeded the supply.
The bearing of these comments and figures on the $48 million is simply this. They tend to show that the western farmers were beaten out of a just remuneration for the wheat they produced and sold. They sold their wheat to Great Britain at $1.55 for the first two years and $2 for the second two years very substantially below the world price of class II wheat. It seems beyond any possibility of dispute that these figures and statements constitute complete proof that the western farmers lost heavily as a result of the agreement, and that they therefore have a claim on the Dominion of Canada for a considerable amount of reimbursement to cover their losses.
Some hon. members have objected to the rest of Canada paying taxes for the benefit of the western farmer. That proposition should be examined, to see whether it is valid. Let me read the statement of Chester A. Bloom, entitled "The Prairie Farmers Pay". This clipping is from the Lethbridge Herald of March 24, 1951. When I referred to this article last spring some members became almost furious, because they implied that Chester A. Bloom was employed by somebody. Their objection quite astonished me, because certainly the figures of Chester A. Bloom must be accurate, no matter whom he is employed by, or whether he is employed by anybody. This is the article:
During the five-year wheat pool including the four-year Canada-U.K. wheat agreement, while selling their wheat to Britain at cut-rate prices, the prairie farmers paid 77 per cent of all the farm income taxes paid in Canada.
During the four years of the U.K. wheat agreement, 1946-49 inclusive, the prairie farmers paid 81 per cent of all the farm income taxes paid in Canada-$48,254,000 out of $59,489,000 farm income taxes.
The farmers of the three prairie provinces were getting gypped two ways-their wheat was sold at bargain prices while they carried more than three-quarters of the farm tax load in Canada.
The answer is easy-their wheat was sold by a government board. The government tax collectors knew every cent of their income-not so with all the other farmers of Canada. No wonder governments like handling farm products through boards.
The 1950 farm tax returns are not yet available. But the prairie farmers have been paying an average of more than $12 million a year in farm income
The Address-Mr. Blackmore
taxes. Their 1950 taxes will surely be up to the average so, during the five-year pool into which the government is now making a $65 million final payment, the prairie farmers will have paid taxes in that period within $5 million of the $65 million.
It is quite obvious why the government did not use these figures to rebut some of the $65 million payment criticisms. It is one of the big national tax scandals of Canada.
Here are some of the figures culled from a return furnished February 22, last, by the Department of National Revenue, answering a question asked in the house by H. R. Argue, M.P., Assiniboia:
In 1946, total farm income taxes collected in Canada were $9,843,000 of which prairie farmers, largely wheat growers, paid $8,134,000 or 82-5 per cent.
1947-	Total Canadian farm income taxes collected, $13,581,000; prairie farmers paid $10,567,000 or 77 per cent.
1948-	Total Canadian farm income taxes collected, $18,095,000; three prairie provinces paid farm income taxes of $14,168,000 or 78 per cent.
1949-	Total Canadian farm income taxes collected, $17,970,000; three prairie provinces farm taxes! $15,385,000 or 85 per cent.
The only provinces which came anywhere near approaching these prairie records of farm income taxes were the immensely wealthy old farming province of Ontario whose farmers in 1949 paid $1,940,000 in farm income taxes while British Columbia farmers paid $544,000. Quebec farmers paid only $51,000. The smaller populated maritime provinces that year paid farm income taxes of: P.E.I., $4,000; Nova Scotia, $33,000; New Brunswick, $11,000, and Newfoundland, $2,000.
Even before the Canadian wheat board had records of prairie farmers' wheat receipts, however, the three prairie provinces were furnishing, since 1941, more than 50 per cent of the total farm income taxes collected in Canada. Here are the records 1941 to 1945 inclusive:
1941-Total farm income taxes collected, $1,592,000; prairie payments, $860,000; 1942-total farm income taxes paid, $3,372,000; prairie payments, $2,045,000; 1943-total for Canada, $11,630,000; prairies paid $8,563,000; 1944-total for Canada, $20,482,000; prairies paid $16,838,000; 1945-total for Canada, $13,392,000; prairies paid $8,047,000.
Anyone who will seriously contemplate those figures should indulge no more in talk about having the rest of Canada pay taxes to help the prairie farmers.
Others have argued as a reason why there should be no payment to western farmers that it was not economically sound to subsidize any group. Let us see what subsidies are paid in Canada. When a tariff is placed on a commodity like a mowing machine which causes the people in a primary producing area to have to pay $25, $30, $40 or $50 more for that machine than they would have to pay if the tariff were not imposed, then that tariff is forcing the primary producers to subsidize the machinery companies. There can be no other interpretation placed upon the effect of the tariff.
I have here an article which indicates a great deal of research in its preparation and which I believe will be quite enlightening to all people who are concerned in this matter, as I think everybody is. It is taken from the

17o2
The Address-Mr. Blackmore Manitoba Co-operator of May 3, 1951 and is entitled "They Talk Subsidies". It is copied from the Alberta wheat pool budget of April 20, 1951, and reads:
The turmoil which has been raised in eastern Canada over the $65 million federal grant to the wheat board to make a final payment of 8-3 cents a bushel for wheat in the 1945-49 pool, is, and should be, resented in western Canada. One would think that the western wheat farmers were mendicants and they alone of all classes in Canada received special treatment. That is far from the case.
H. H. Hannam, president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, has listed some federal government subsidy payments made to groups and industries other than farmers, in the 1949-50 fiscal year
as follows:
Subsidy for Canadian gold mines	 $13,715,778
Subsidy on movement of coal	 3,919,000
Subsidy on steel and iron	 4,662,251
For unemployment insurance	 45,059,588
Subsidy for judges' (114) pensions	 458,937
Then special depreciation on $514 million invested was allowed war industry during world war II.
The Canadian tariff in itself operates in the nature of a bonus to Canadian industries and is oppressive particularly to people residing in the prairie provinces of western Canada. In the early 1930's the late Hon. Norman Rogers, Minister of Labour in the Canadian government, prepared a table showing how each province in Canada was affected by the dominion's tariff policy.
That table showed that at that time the Canadian tariffs cost the people of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta $54,925,000 a year, or an annual average charge of $23 on every man, woman and child in the three provinces. With the expansion of Canadian industry and western purchasing, the figures may now be doubled.
The table also showed that the provinces of Ontario and Quebec had an annual gain through the tariff of $83,700,000.
The $65 million grant by the federal government to the wheat board permits a payment of 41 cents a bushel on 1,436,000,000 bushels of wheat delivered by the farmers of western Canada between 1945 and 1949 inclusive. It brings the total payment up to a little over $1.83 a bushel, basis 1 Northern at the terminal, on total deliveries.
Between March 1, 1945, and February 17, 1947, the wheat board sold 160 million bushels of wheat for domestic consumption at $1.25 a bushel when the export price was $1.55. That was a direct subsidy by the wheat producers to Canadian consumers to the extent of $48 million.
The prairie provinces of western Canada constitute a land area of 452 million acres, of which 117 million are in occupied farms; 65 million acres being improved lands. This is one of the most productive farming regions in the world.
During the war this area produced nearly 5,500,000,000 bushels of grain, over 5 billion pounds of beef, and 8,600,000 pounds of pork. This production resulted in Canadian people being among the best fed in the world, and also provided 3,100,000,000 pounds of pork and 600 million pounds of beef for export to Great Britain.
While Canada has experienced a growing industrialism, which strengthens the nation's economic fabric, agricultural production is still the mainstay of the national economy. The farmers of western Canada, under the constant risk of drouth, hail and insect pests, have rendered an exceptional contribution to the progress of the Canadian nation. "Without a west" Canada would not be much of a nation.
In the light of the figures I have placed upon the record during this talk I think it

will be realized that western farmers are most moderate when they come to this parliament asking for compensation for the amount of money they lost as a result of sales of wheat under the British-Canadian wheat agreement, and especially their argument that they are entitled to this $48 million as reimbursement for their loss in subsidizing Canadian bread consumers.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. J. Browne (Si. John's West):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question agitating the minds of most people in Canada for the last year has been the high cost of living. One reason for the higher cost this year has been the high taxation imposed by the government. This was well pointed out this afternoon by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker) and also by no less a person than the president of the Bank of Montreal in his recent annual statement to the shareholders. He pointed out that the government through its policy of high taxation was contributing to the increase in the cost of living. This was also pointed out by speakers on the opposition side last year when these extra taxes were put on articles which everyone recognized to be necessaries of life. Therefore the government cannot escape the just accusation that they are responsible to a large extent for the figure the cost of living index has now reached.
This increase in the cost of living falls in various degrees upon different persons. There are some people who have the advantage of working agreements containing escalator clauses so that as the cost of living index rises their wages or salaries also rise. Those people who are getting their income from profits find that those profits are increasing in proportion to the cost of merchandise which they sell. Although they do lag behind somewhat, civil servants get bonuses. But there is a class of person about whom I wish to speak tonight who has very little opportunity of redress and who must depend to a large extent upon government assistance. I intend to speak about the Newfoundland fishermen.
It is a strange anomaly that fish, salted codfish at any rate, is one of the food products in the world that has gone down in price during the past two years. This means that the return to the fisherman is less than it was, whereas the cost of the articles he must use has gone up. In other words his cost of catching fish has increased and the value of fish has gone down.
As hon. members know, in 1949 Newfoundland came into confederation. There were

many who thought this would be most beneficial to all concerned, but it has not proved beneficial to the fisherman, as I intend to point out. In 1948 the fishermen of Newfoundland received their highest prices for fish, about $13.45 for small madeira fish. In 1949 it began that way, but they could not sell their fish and the result was that there was a carryover into the season of 1950. The fisheries prices support board had to come to their assistance to a certain extent. That assistance was not very great, but they had to buy several thousand quintals of fish from the fishermen. However, 1950 was the worst season for many years. The initial price was nearly $3 a quintal lower. I suppose I should explain to hon. members what I mean by a quintal. A quintal is 112 pounds or a hundredweight of fish. The bureau of statistics does not use that figure. They use a figure of 100 pounds, but we refer to a quintal of 112 pounds. In the 1950 season the price started off at only $10.50 for small madeira fish for which $13.45 was paid the year before. There was a difference of nearly $3 a quintal or 3 cents a pound in the price of the fish.
This was bound to have an effect upon the fishermen. But that was the highest price paid during the year, and it began to drop after the month of September. Those who were not fortunate enough to get their fish sold during September had to accept a lower price. I have already brought the prices paid in 1950 to the attention of the house. Fish sold after September averaged as low as $5.50, which is only about half the better price paid in September. The men could not make a living and the provincial government instituted an inquiry to see if the merchants were paying fair and just prices. The fisheries prices support board had an investigation, and some hon. members may recall that it was decided, so far as Labrador fish are concerned, to guarantee a price of $7 a quintal, to which a supplementary amount of 85 cents has since been added in the case of semi-dry fish. Therefore some Labrador fishermen will receive a guaranteed price of $7.85.
Labrador fish is not the superior article that shore fish is and usually commands only 60 to 75 per cent in value by way of return. But with respect to the shore fish the fisheries prices support board has recommended to the government that a deficiency payment of $1.30 per quintal, a little over one cent a pound, be paid to all fishermen independently of the price they may have received. I know some fishermen who received top prices. They were good fishermen and were lucky. They got their fish on the market at the beginning of the season and received top prices. They
The Address-Mr. W. J. Browne will also get $1.30, but those unfortunate enough to live a long distance away from the city of St. John's, where the top price was paid in September, those who were unfortunate enough to have bad weather in their communities so they could not make their fish in time, received low prices and the same deficiency payment of $1.30.
As I mentioned, some of them received an average of $5.50. They will get $1.30 added to that. It will be seen that $1.30 added to their $5.50 is very far removed from what the man will get who received the top price of $10.50 and has $1.30 added to that. I suppose the fisheries prices support board gave the matter long and careful consideration and felt that the only practical way to solve the problem was to give everybody $1.30 regardless of how much they had been able to get for their fish. The effect of the depressed prices last year was to drive a lot of people out of the fisheries. They could not go fishing this year. They gave it up. Some of them went to Goose Bay, some to Seven Islands, and others have gone to Greenland. Others have gone wherever they could find work. Some of them are working in the government-owned industries now being started under the new policy of the provincial government. The $1.30 has not yet been paid for the 1950 catch, and we are getting near the end of 1951. I do not know how the government thinks the people who received a little over 5 cents a pound for their fish last year have been living. The amount of $1.30 is not going to be paid until January. I have been asking questions in the house about the matter during the time the house has been in session, and it is always put off a couple of months ahead. Now at last in the new year I suppose the fishermen will begin to get $1.30.

speechtext:
I do not
know if it is going to be before the election. I do not think it will amount to enough to influence the election down there. We come to the 1951 catch, and in many places this year the catch was good. It was better than in 1950, but not so with regard to the Labrador fisheries because most of the people who had been fishing there did not go there this year. There are two classes of fishermen who fish at Labrador. One is called the livyers, people who live there and fish, and the others are floaters who go there in large vessels. To a great extent the large vessels have abandoned the Labrador fishing. For them it is a thing of the past. It does not pay them to go there any more. They

The Address-Mr. W. J. Browne have given it up and the government does not seem to be the least bit worried about whether or not they give it up.
But there are other fishermen whom I met recently and whom I also met in 1949, and about whom I can tell a story and give a comparison. In 1949 I was in the village of Ship Harbour on Placentia bay in my constituency. I was in a house there, and as I was having tea a vessel came in from the banks loaded to the gunwales. Everybody was delighted. I was in that same village three weeks ago in the same house. The man who was captain of the vessel that had come in with a load of fish in 1949 was sitting at the table twiddling his thumbs. He was not fishing this year. He had two vessels tied up to his wharf all summer. He had seven traps in the holds. He said to me: "I cannot give that stuff away; I cannot sell those traps for 25 cents, although I have $9,000 worth of material there."
Is the federal government really interested in the fishermen of Newfoundland? Is it really interested in the fisheries of Newfoundland? The minister is a brave man and has received a ribbon of honour for his visit to the Korean battlefront. I know he is a sympathetic person; but does he really intelligently understand the fisheries of Newfoundland? I doubt it. His parliamentary assistant lives nearer and ought to know more about it, but he has not the authority. It is necessary for the government to remember that they have to give a lot more consideration and attention to the fisheries of Newfoundland than they have shown during the last two and a half years if they do not want them to decline. I received a letter only a few days ago from a very fine fisherman who has been in the fisheries all his life. He lives in a fishing village on Placentia bay, and he tells me that men are going to leave the fisheries in greater numbers this coming season. He also stresses the point that although there was a good catch in many places this year the weather was bad and the cull is hard. That means that the inspectors of the merchants, or cullers las we call them, the men who pick out and1 grade the fish, <are very strict, and the quantity of the higher priced fish is much smaller in proportion, Therefore the men are in exactly the same position as they were in 1950.
I call upon the government now to instruct the fisheries prices support board to recognize that situation, because it is equally necessary for them to give a deficiency payment for the 1951 catch as it was for the 1950 catch. I have here the report of the fisheries prices support board for the year 1950-51, which contains a resume of the purposes of the act. I should like to put it on the record to remind


hon. members that I am not asking for anything of an extraordinary nature when I ask the government now to give consideration to making a deficiency payment on the 1951 catch of salt codfish in Newfoundland. The report has this to say:
The act which came into force in July, 1947, gives the fisheries prices support board the usual powers of a government corporation; provides a working fund of $25 million; and sets out the two methods that may be used to support prices of fisheries products. These methods are (a) the purchase of any fisheries product at a prescribed price and (b) the making of deficiency payments to producers of a fisheries product equal to the difference between a prescribed price and the average price at which such product was sold during a specified period.
Now, sir, that is what was done for the 1950 catch. The government set the prescribed price for which this fish should have been sold. They said it was $10.10, and the average price received by the fishermen was $8.80. Subtract $8.80 from $10.10, and you get $1.30. I continue:
The act furthermore directs that in prescribing prices, the board shall endeavour to ensure adequate and stable returns for fisheries by promoting orderly adjustment from war to peace conditions and shall endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns from fisheries and those from other occupations.
That was a very laudable object which the fisheries prices support board had in mind. I do not think they made a proper adjustment for the 1950 catch by giving $1.30 to a man who had received an average of $5.50. I do hope that this year they will profit by the experience of the past year and be a little .more generous in their recommendations.
But, sir, that is not all about the fisheries. I do not suppose many hon. members in the house are familiar with the manifesto issued by the present premier of Newfoundland prior to the election that took place there on November 26. If they had been able to see that manifesto I think they would have been astonished, if they knew anything about the history of Newfoundland, because one of the policies outlined in this extraordinary manifesto is to take 10,000 men out of the fisheries and put them to work in factories. Anyone who has any knowledge of economics or sound economy for any country must realize that that is revolution. The number of people engaged in the fisheries last year could not have been much over 20,000. Perhaps the parliamentary assistant might know the figure, but I think it would be in the neighbourhood of 20,000. To take half the fishermen out of the fisheries and put them at jobs in factories would mean what? What would be the result? What would be the effect on the fisheries? Is it going to make the fisheries better? The premier of Newfoundland thinks

he is going to put new life into the fisheries by taking 10,000, or half the people, out of them. That is not all. I mention this not from the political standpoint but purely from the economic standpoint, and to draw the attention of the government and the officials concerned in the fisheries department to the policy being enunciated by the premier of Newfoundland. He says the men, women and children, the fishermen, their wives and their families, must be taken away from the slavery of making fish. That was the first time I had ever heard of fishermen being regarded as slaves. I have often heard of wage slaves, of people working in factories living like slaves, but I never heard of fishermen living like slaves, and I do not think it is a sound or sensible statement.
Again, the reason I am drawing it to the attention of the federal government is that this government has a paramount interest in the fisheries of Newfoundland. I do not know what the present policy of the federal government is, but fisheries come under its jurisdiction. What does it say in regard to the policies enunciated by the premier of Newfoundland? The fisheries board of Newfoundland is going to continue to operate for five years, but after that who is going to take over the management of the fisheries? Is it the federal government? Are they going to have anything to say in the meantime? Will the pattern be cut and finished when they take over in another two and a half years? I know the minister has expressed an interest and sympathy. He has advocated an advertising program. I believe he started a kitchen to show people how fish should be cooked, and only today I received a very pleasant surprise, namely a little book of fish recipes, telling us how to cook fish, anything from lobster to salmon, cod and herring.

speechtext:
I have tried to encourage the minister to have confidence in the fisheries; to get him to realize that the salt cod fishery is not a dying industry; that it is a most important industry in Newfoundland still. Despite all this industrialization program of the provincial government, the salt codfish industry remains an industry that has the most far-reaching effect. If hon. gentlemen could have seen the happy look on the faces of fishermen whom I met in the northern parts of Newfoundland last year when they were taking in hundreds of quintals of fish they would have realized the beneficial influence which a good cod fishery has upon the people. I do not know what they are feeling like now with the market depressed and prices low, but I am satisfied that the government has not been doing all that it might do to assist in the marketing of codfish. I noticed that two years ago we sold several thousand quintals of fish to Spain. None was sold last year. Although we were told that a contract was being negotiated, it never came through.
Spain used to be the best market for Newfoundland codfish, taking as high as 375,000 quintals a year. Last year they took none. Does anyone think for a moment that the Spanish people are not eating salt codfish? Of course they are. They are catching some of it themselves, and perhaps they are buying more-I believe they are-from Norway. Therefore there is a market there still which has to be negotiated. The minister told me on one occasion that Spain had a favourable balance of trade with this country. There is something to work on. There are other things which may be purchased in Spain, so that we might have a reciprocal trade agreement with that country. It is a country with a very large population, much larger than Portugal, which takes a great deal of fish, while Spain takes none. I therefore urge the government to explore every avenue to try to sell codfish in Spain.
Brazil is another market that began to deteriorate back nine or ten years ago, and we have not been selling much fish to Brazil. Certainly the government cannot overlook the fact that these countries regard salt codfish as a highly desirable food. It can be so well preserved and carried from place to place, and therefore there must be a need for it if they would only arrange the transaction. I do not say that it is an easy thing to do, but I think there may be a lot more done than has been done in the past.
To go back to this policy enunciated by the premier, of taking 10,000 men out of fisheries; what would be the effect of a policy such as that? Not only 10,000 men would go from the villages, but their families would go from them. Thirty or forty thousand

The Address-Mr. W. J. Browne people would be taken out of those fishing communities and would go to the city of St. John's or wherever these industries are started, and live in crowded quarters, tenements and that sort of thing. They would not have the happiness of living in their own homes, and their property would deteriorate. I have a question on the order paper asking the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) about how much money is being lent outside the city of St. John's. I do not think any money is being lent to these fishing communities to make the homes more attractive to the families of fishermen. It seems to me that if the people in the maritimes or in the west can complain about the amount of money that is going to be spent on the seaway project, then the fishermen in all parts of this country have some cause for complaint. They live in isolated communities, and see grand houses being built in the cities while no money is being lent to them to improve their living conditions. What will happen to the schools, churches and local amenities that have to be kept up by contributions from the fishermen if half the population is taken away? It seems to me to be a suicidal policy, and I believe the man who advocates it will find he has made a tremendous mistake.
In addition to those ideas I have mentioned, he also suggested in his manifesto that instead of the traditional way in which the fishery has been conducted he is going to introduce another revolution in the curing of fish. Instead of the individual fisherman going through the various stages of curing and selling his fish, as he has done in the past, the government is going to set up a central curing establishment to which the fishermen will bring their fresh fish. There it will be treated and cured, and from there it will be marketed. This sounds like a plausible scheme, but unless it is a co-operative project in which the fisherman will get his share of the profit or benefit as a result of working through this agency, then he will be even worse off than he is today. He will receive only the price for his fresh fish, which of course is the lowest price at which the commodity is sold. Naturally when the fish just comes out of the water it has a lower value than after it has been processed, salted and dried. In that way the fisherman's family add to the value of the fish and add to their income. If the policy of establishing this central curing agency is pursued it will not only destroy the independence of the fishermen but will make them far more dependent upon government assistance than they have ever been in the past.
On occasions I believe the federal government, as well as other people, have made

reference to the change that is taking place in the cod fishery due to the expansion of the fresh and frozen fish market, especially in the United States. It is a tonic, therefore, to realize that in the past few days New England interests have been appearing before the United States tariff commission demanding an increase in the tariff on fresh fish imported into the United States. I say that is a tonic because it is a reminder to those people who are placing so much confidence in the United States market that this market may be lost over night. The difference of a half a cent a pound may ruin that market for us, and the tariff may be raised more than that. Next year is an election year in the United States, and it is possible that the tariff commission may do something to satisfy the New England interests who have always been jealous of the sales made by the Nova Scotia and Newfoundland fishermen in the United States market. I noticed, too, that not only Nova Scotia and Newfoundland fish is going into this market, but since 1948 the Norwegians have been selling frozen codfish in the United States market. Although in 1948 they sold only a small quantity, about $85,000 worth, this year the value of the fish sold was over $2 million. In the salt codfish markets of the world Newfoundland has been faced with Norwegian competition, and now Norway is going into the fresh fish market of the United States.
It would not be wise for the government to depend too much upon the expansion of the fresh fish market. In Newfoundland we are going to get two or three new plants this year, and several new draggers have been built or purchased during the past year. The federal government is experimenting wih new ways of catching fish. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the chief problem facing the salt cod fishery is the marketing of salt codfish. The government need not be so worried about the question of catching the codfish. I believe the Newfoundlanders know how to catch codfish if the government can only assist them in marketing it. We have these new plants, these new vessels and these new methods, but I think it is a dangerous policy to allow the salt cod fishery to decline in the way it has during the past three years.
